distractorExplanations.a: Uses length of coverage first. That tie-breaker is reached only when no active-employee rule already names the plan that pays first.
distractorExplanations.b: Reverses the order. A retiree plan from a former employer pays after the plan that covers her as an active worker.
distractorExplanations.c: Splits the bill in half. Coordination names one primary plan, and the active-worker plan takes that place.

prompt: Sam has met his deductible. His in-network surgeon bills $6,000 for a covered operation. The plan's allowed amount is $4,000, and the surgeon agreed to accept that amount. The plan pays 80% of the allowed amount, and the policy states no copay for this operation. What does Sam owe the surgeon?

options.text: $800, which is 20% of the allowed amount
$1,200, which is 20% of the $6,000 bill
$2,800, the coinsurance plus the $2,000 above the allowed amount
$6,000, the surgeon's full bill, because a network agreement does not limit what he collects

explanation: An in-network surgeon who accepts the allowed amount does not bill Sam the extra $2,000. The plan pays 80% of the $4,000 allowed amount, which is $3,200. Sam's coinsurance is the other 20%, which is $800. The policy states no copay, and the deductible is already met, so Sam owes $800.

distractorExplanations.b: Takes 20% of the $6,000 billed charge, which is $1,200. In network, coinsurance uses the $4,000 allowed amount, so Sam's share is $800.
distractorExplanations.c: Adds the $2,000 above the allowed amount to the coinsurance. The surgeon agreed to accept $4,000, so Sam does not pay that $2,000.
distractorExplanations.d: Lets the surgeon collect the full $6,000. Accepting the allowed amount limits the covered charge to $4,000 before the 80% plan payment.

prompt: Paula is 66 and still working. She has Medicare and the group health plan at her job. That employer has 40 employees. A covered physician bill is sent to both payers. Which payer pays first?

options.text: Medicare, because it becomes the first payer on the 65th birthday
Her employer's group health plan
Whichever payer has covered her for more years
The two payers, in equal shares, because she still works after 65

explanation: When a person age 65 or older is still working, the employer group health plan pays before Medicare if that employer has 20 or more employees. Paula is 66, and her employer has 40 employees, so the group plan pays this bill first. Medicare pays second. Age 66 alone does not put Medicare first.

distractorExplanations.a: Makes Medicare first at age 65 in every case. With 40 employees, the group plan of a working 66-year-old pays before Medicare.
distractorExplanations.c: Uses length of coverage to rank the payers. Employer size decides this case, and 40 employees puts the group plan first.
distractorExplanations.d: Splits the bill in equal shares. One payer is primary. The employer plan pays first because the employer has more than 20 employees.

prompt: Greta can see an in-network specialist without a referral. A routine visit to a physician outside the network is not paid, while emergency care is paid. Which managed-care plan matches those rules?

options.text: A preferred provider plan, because it pays nothing for routine care outside the network
A health maintenance organization, because it waives referrals and still bars routine outside care
An exclusive provider organization
A point-of-service plan, because a routine visit outside the network is left unpaid

explanation: An exclusive provider organization pays in-network care, generally with no referral, and does not pay a routine out-of-network visit. Emergency care remains covered. That is the pattern Greta's plan uses. A preferred provider plan would still pay a reduced benefit for the routine outside visit.

distractorExplanations.a: Describes the opposite of a preferred provider plan. That plan still pays a reduced benefit for a routine visit outside the network.
distractorExplanations.b: Assigns the pattern to a health maintenance organization. That plan typically requires a primary-care referral before a specialist visit, and Greta's plan does not.
distractorExplanations.d: Assigns the pattern to a point-of-service plan. That plan pays routine care outside the network at a higher member share. It does not leave the visit unpaid.

prompt: Malik wants medical coverage with no contracted physician panel. He wants any licensed doctor to be available, with covered charges reimbursed after a deductible and coinsurance. Which plan is built that way?

options.text: A health maintenance organization, because members may visit any doctor and then file a claim
A preferred provider plan, because it keeps no list of contracted physicians
An exclusive provider organization, because doctors off the panel are reimbursed at the same level
An indemnity plan

explanation: An indemnity plan, also called fee-for-service, has no contracted physician panel. The insured may see any licensed doctor, and the insurer reimburses covered charges after the deductible and coinsurance. Managed-care plans contract with a panel and steer members toward those doctors.

distractorExplanations.a: Gives a health maintenance organization an open choice of doctors. That plan generally pays its own panel, with emergency care as the usual exception.
distractorExplanations.b: Says a preferred provider plan has no contracted physicians. It does. Care inside that panel is paid at a higher level than care outside it.
distractorExplanations.c: Says an exclusive provider organization reimburses any doctor at the same level. It generally pays no routine benefit to a doctor off its panel.

prompt: A group medical plan states that a nonemergency hospital admission must be precertified. If it is not, the plan pays 50% of the covered charge instead of its usual 80%. Camille is admitted for scheduled surgery and does not call. The stay is otherwise covered, and she has met the deductible. What share does the plan pay?

options.text: 50% of the covered charge
80% of the covered charge, because the lower share applies only to an emergency admission
Nothing, because skipping the call cancels coverage for the whole stay
The full covered charge, because meeting the deductible removes the reduction

explanation: Precertification is the plan's advance review of a nonemergency admission. This plan states the result of skipping it: the plan pays 50% of the covered charge instead of 80%. Camille's surgery was scheduled and she did not call, so the plan pays 50%. A met deductible does not restore the 80% share, and the stay is not denied in full.

distractorExplanations.b: Applies the 50% reduction to emergencies and keeps 80% here. The plan states the 50% share for a nonemergency admission that was not precertified.
distractorExplanations.c: Turns the stated penalty into a total denial. The plan still pays 50% of the covered charge. It does not refuse the whole stay.
distractorExplanations.d: Treats the met deductible as if it erased the reduction. The plan pays 50%, not the full charge, when required precertification was skipped.

prompt: Ned was laid off and elected continuation coverage on the former employer's medical plan. The same month, a new employer enrolls him in its plan for active workers. Today's claim is eligible under both. Which plan pays first?

options.text: The continuation plan, because it stays primary through the first month of a new job
The active plan at the new job
The continuation plan, because he has been on the former employer's coverage longer
Each plan pays half of the claim until he drops one of them

explanation: When someone is covered as an active employee and also has continuation coverage from a former employer, the active plan pays first. Ned's new-job plan is primary, and the continuation plan pays second. A longer history on the former plan does not reverse that order.

distractorExplanations.a: Keeps continuation coverage primary during the first month. It pays after a plan that covers him as an active employee, including in that month.
distractorExplanations.c: Uses length of coverage. The active-employee rule already makes the new-job plan pay first, so the longer former coverage does not control.
distractorExplanations.d: Splits the claim in half. Coordination names one primary plan, and the active plan at the new job pays first.

prompt: Chris has a major medical plan with a $400 deductible and 75/25 coinsurance. Nothing has been credited to the deductible this year. His only claim is a covered surgery with an allowed charge of $2,400. How much does Chris pay?
explanation: The plan pays 75% and Chris pays 25% after the deductible. He pays the $400 deductible first, leaving $2,400 - $400 = $2,000. His coinsurance is 0.25 times $2,000 = $500. His total is $400 + $500 = $900. The plan pays 0.75 times $2,000 = $1,500.

distractorExplanations.b: Stops at the deductible. He also owes 25% of the remaining $2,000, which is $500, so $400 is not his full payment.
distractorExplanations.c: Takes 25% of the full $2,400, which is $600, and skips the deductible. Coinsurance applies only after the $400 is removed.
distractorExplanations.d: Names the plan's share, 0.75 times $2,000 = $1,500, rather than Chris's $900. Reversing 75/25 swaps his bill with the plan's.

prompt: Greta's medical plan pays 80% of the allowed amount after the deductible. She chooses an out-of-network clinic, and the contract imposes a 20-percentage-point network penalty on the plan's share. The allowed amount is $1,000 and the deductible is already met. How much does the plan pay?
explanation: The network penalty cuts the plan's share from 80% to 60% because 80 - 20 = 60. The deductible is already met, so no further amount is subtracted before the percentage. The plan pays 0.60 times $1,000 = $600. Greta owes the other $400 of the allowed amount.

distractorExplanations.a: Uses the in-network 80% and ignores the network penalty. Out of network, 80 minus 20 points leaves 60%, so the plan pays $600, not $800.
distractorExplanations.c: Treats the 20-point penalty as the benefit. The penalty is a reduction, not the payment; 0.20 times $1,000 is only $200.
distractorExplanations.d: Assumes a met deductible makes the plan pay the full allowed amount. The plan still pays 60% of $1,000, which is $600, not $1,000.

prompt: Ruth keeps Original Medicare and adds a Medicare supplement. Medicare approves a covered hospital stay but leaves her with cost-sharing under Parts A and B. Conceptually, what is that supplement designed to do?

options.text: Replace Parts A and B so Medicare stops paying the hospital
Act as her drug plan instead of helping with hospital cost-sharing
Help pay included Medicare cost-sharing while Medicare stays primary
Drop Original Medicare and run the stay as a private network plan with drug coverage added on

explanation: A Medicare supplement is built to sit beside Original Medicare, not to replace it. It helps pay cost-sharing Medicare leaves to the patient, such as deductibles and coinsurance, but only the pieces that the supplement's benefits include. Medicare still processes the covered stay.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a supplement with a private plan that replaces Medicare. A supplement does not cancel Parts A and B or stop Medicare from paying its share.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses the supplement with outpatient drug coverage. Helping with hospital and medical cost-sharing is not the same as becoming a pharmacy benefit.
distractorExplanations.d: Describes leaving Original Medicare for a replacement plan. A supplement keeps Medicare primary and only helps with cost-sharing the supplement includes.

prompt: Neil's individual medical policy says the premium is due on the first of each month and states a 10-day grace period. The March premium is unpaid when he receives covered care on March 7. He pays that premium on March 9. How is the March 7 claim treated?

options.text: Denied, because coverage ended on the due date and the later payment cannot restore the March 7 claim
Covered when the loss is an injury, because this grace period is described as accident-only
Postponed until a reinstatement application is approved and a new waiting period ends
Covered, because the care and the payment both fall inside the stated grace period

explanation: The policy states a 10-day grace period, so it stays in force while the overdue premium can still be paid. From the March 1 due date, March 7 is 7 - 1 = 6 days later and March 9 is 9 - 1 = 8 days later. Both 6 and 8 are less than 10, so the policy was still in force on March 7. He paid the premium on March 9, which is also inside the 10 days, so the March 7 claim is covered and the policy did not lapse.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats the due date as a lapse. The stated 10-day grace period keeps the policy in force, and both day 6 and day 8 of the delay fall inside those 10 days.
distractorExplanations.b: Limits the grace period to injuries. The policy states a 10-day grace period for the premium, and the March 7 care is covered without that accident-only limit.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses the grace period with reinstatement. He paid on day 8 of a 10-day period, so the policy never lapsed and no new application is required.

prompt: Lila's major medical policy carries deductible credit from October, November, and December into the next calendar year. A November claim counted $350 toward her deductible. The new year's deductible is $700, and she has had no claim yet in January. How much of that new deductible is still unmet on January 1?
explanation: The carryover applies the November credit against the new deductible rather than erasing it or adding to it. Subtract: $700 - $350 = $350 still unmet on January 1. She has had no January claim, so nothing further has been credited.

distractorExplanations.b: Treats a partial credit as full satisfaction. Only $350 carried over, so $700 - $350 = $350 remains; the new deductible is not down to $0.
distractorExplanations.c: Drops the carryover when the year changes. The policy keeps the November $350, so the unmet amount is $350, not a fresh $700.
distractorExplanations.d: Adds the credit instead of applying it. $700 + $350 = $1,050 would raise the deductible; the carryover reduces it to $350.

prompt: The Ruiz family medical plan sets a $500 deductible per person and includes a common-accident provision. Two covered children are injured in the same crash. Each child's covered treatment is $800. How much deductible applies to this crash in total?
explanation: A common-accident provision applies one deductible when more than one covered family member is hurt in the same accident. Charging each child would be $500 times 2 = $1,000, but the provision uses one deductible of $500. The treatment totals $800 + $800 = $1,600, which shows the deductible can be met; that sum is not the deductible.

distractorExplanations.a: Waives the deductible down to $0. The provision limits this crash to one deductible; it does not erase the $500 charge.
distractorExplanations.c: Charges each child a separate deductible. That mistake produces $500 + $500 = $1,000, which is the result the common-accident provision avoids.
distractorExplanations.d: Uses the combined treatment as the deductible. $800 + $800 = $1,600 is the covered care, not the $500 deductible the plan applies once.

prompt: Omar's individual medical policy is effective June 1 and states a 30-day probationary period for sickness. He injures an ankle in a fall on June 10 and is diagnosed with influenza on June 20. Which of these losses can the policy cover?

options.text: Both the ankle injury and the influenza, since the contract is already in force
Only the influenza, since the probationary period delays accident benefits
Only the ankle injury
Neither loss, since no benefit is payable until the full probationary period ends

explanation: A probationary period delays sickness coverage; accident coverage starts on the effective date. June 10 is 10 - 1 = 9 days after June 1, and the ankle injury is an accident, so the 30-day sickness wait does not apply. June 20 is 20 - 1 = 19 days after June 1. Because 19 is less than 30, the influenza is still inside the sickness probation and is not covered.

distractorExplanations.a: Ignores the sickness probation. The contract is in force, but influenza on day 19 is still inside the 30-day sickness wait, so only the accident can be covered.
distractorExplanations.b: Reverses the probationary period. It delays sickness, not accidents, so the June 10 fall is the loss the policy can cover.
distractorExplanations.d: Applies the 30-day wait to every loss. Accidents are covered from June 1; this wait is for sickness, and day 9 is already an accident claim.

prompt: Helena owns a major medical policy that is guaranteed renewable to age 65. After several large claims, the insurer wants to drop her alone and leave every other insured in that class unchanged. What may the insurer do?

options.text: Cancel her policy at renewal and keep every other insured in the class on the same form
Renew her policy but price her from her own claims while the class rate stays unchanged
Nonrenew her at will, because guaranteed renewable locks the terms for the first year only
Renew her policy and limit any rate change to the class as a whole

explanation: Guaranteed renewable means the insurer must renew until the age stated in the policy if premiums are paid. That age is 65. Dropping Helena alone because of her claims substitutes a cancellation for renewal up to age 65. A rate change has to apply to the whole class. Treating the promise as a one-year lock would require 65 to equal 1, and it does not.

distractorExplanations.a: Cancels one insured for heavy claims. Guaranteed renewable to age 65 requires renewal of her policy; the insurer cannot drop her and keep the rest of the class.
distractorExplanations.b: Reprices one person from her own claims. On this policy a rate change applies to the class, not to a single insured who has not yet reached age 65.
distractorExplanations.c: Cuts the guarantee off after the first year. The contract runs to age 65, and 65 does not equal a one-year term, so claims are not grounds to nonrenew her.

prompt: A basic surgical expense policy pays from a set schedule and has no coinsurance percentage. The schedule allows $900 for Nia's procedure. The surgeon bills $1,400. How much does this policy pay?
explanation: A scheduled surgical policy pays the listed amount for the procedure. The schedule allows $900, so the policy pays $900, not the $1,400 bill. The unpaid difference is $1,400 - $900 = $500. Averaging the two figures would be ($900 + $1,400) / 2 = $1,150, which the schedule does not do.

distractorExplanations.b: Pays the billed charge. The schedule caps this procedure at $900; the extra $500 of the $1,400 bill is not a scheduled benefit.
distractorExplanations.c: Pays the excess instead of the allowance. $1,400 - $900 = $500 is the amount left unpaid; the policy benefit is the $900 schedule amount.
distractorExplanations.d: Averages the schedule and the bill. ($900 + $1,400) / 2 = $1,150 is not the benefit; the policy pays the listed $900.

prompt: Bea is enrolled in her employer's group major medical plan. She fractures a wrist while running a press on the job, and workers' compensation covers that injury. How should the group medical plan treat the wrist care?

options.text: Pay the wrist care as primary and leave workers' compensation to fund only a remainder
Leave the work injury to workers' compensation
Split the wrist bill equally with workers' compensation because both apply
Pay the medical bills for the wrist and leave only lost wages to workers' compensation

explanation: Group major medical coverage excludes an occupational injury that workers' compensation covers. Bea was hurt while running a press at work, and workers' compensation accepts the injury, so the group plan does not pay that care as primary and does not split the bill with the compensation carrier. Workers' compensation pays the medical care for that injury, not lost wages alone.

distractorExplanations.a: Reverses the order of payment. A work injury accepted by workers' compensation falls under the group plan's occupational exclusion, so the group plan is not primary.
distractorExplanations.c: Invents an equal split between the two coverages. Both being in force does not make them share an occupational injury the medical plan excludes.
distractorExplanations.d: Limits workers' compensation to lost wages. It also pays the medical care for this work injury, so the group plan does not pay the wrist bills.

prompt: A group health plan that covers maternity wants to cap a mother's hospital stay at 24 hours after a vaginal birth. Under the Newborns' and Mothers' Health Protection Act, what stay must the plan generally cover for that birth?

options.text: 24 hours, the cap written in the plan, because federal law uses the plan's own limit
No hour minimum, because the mother and her provider may agree to an earlier discharge
At least 48 hours
At least 96 hours, the minimum that applies to a cesarean and to a vaginal birth alike

explanation: For a vaginal delivery, the plan must generally cover at least 48 hours in the hospital. The plan's 24-hour cap is short by 48 - 24 = 24 hours. A 96-hour minimum applies to a cesarean delivery, not to this vaginal birth. The mother and her provider may agree to leave earlier, and that agreement does not reduce the 48 hours the plan must cover.

distractorExplanations.a: Lets the plan's 24-hour cap control. The federal minimum for a vaginal birth is 48 hours, and 48 - 24 = 24, so a 24-hour contractual cap is not enough.
distractorExplanations.b: Treats an agreed early discharge as erasing the minimum. They may leave sooner, but the plan must still cover at least 48 hours for this vaginal birth.
distractorExplanations.d: Uses the cesarean figure for every birth. The 96-hour minimum is for a cesarean; this vaginal birth is held to 48 hours.

prompt: Eli has covered surgery at an in-network hospital. The anesthesiologist is outside the network and bills $2,200 above the plan's allowed amount for that ancillary service. Under the federal No Surprises Act, how much of this extra $2,200 may be collected from Eli?

options.text: The $2,200 extra when no balance-billing consent is on file

explanation: An out-of-network anesthesiologist at an in-network hospital is an ancillary provider under the No Surprises Act, so Eli is protected from that balance bill. Of the extra $2,200, the amount collectible from him is $2,200 - $2,200 = $0. Half of the surplus would be $2,200 / 2 = $1,100, and that split is not his share. Consent does not change the result: this ancillary service cannot be balance billed.

distractorExplanations.a: Allows a balance bill of the full $2,200. For this ancillary service at an in-network facility, the act bars the anesthesiologist from collecting that extra from Eli.
distractorExplanations.b: Splits the surplus in half. $2,200 / 2 = $1,100 is not his balance-bill share; the extra amount collectible from him is $0.
distractorExplanations.c: Treats a missing consent as permission to collect the surplus. Ancillary anesthesia at an in-network hospital cannot be balance billed, so Eli owes none of the extra $2,200.

prompt: After 12 years on her employer's group medical plan, Camille leaves the job and does not elect continuation coverage. The plan contains a conversion privilege. What does that privilege let her obtain?

options.text: Twelve additional months on the employer plan with the employer still paying its share
Repayment of what was paid for group coverage across those 12 years
An individual medical policy without evidence of insurability
Medicare enrollment based solely on those 12 years of employer medical coverage

explanation: A conversion privilege lets her buy an individual medical policy without evidence of insurability. She was covered for 12 years. Those 12 years are the group history being converted; they are not repaid, and they are not extended by 12 more months on the employer plan. Counting 12 years also does not by itself meet a Medicare eligibility test.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses conversion with staying on the group plan. Conversion issues an individual policy; it does not add 12 months of employer coverage to the 12 years she already had.
distractorExplanations.b: Invents repayment of amounts paid over 12 years. The privilege is an individual policy without health evidence, not money returned for those years.
distractorExplanations.d: Treats 12 years of group enrollment as a Medicare qualifier. Conversion produces an individual medical policy, and those 12 years do not by themselves enroll her in Medicare.

prompt: A 35-year-old parent wants the lowest premium for $500,000 of coverage that stays the same for 20 years while the children grow up. Which policy fits best?

options.text: Straight whole life
Single-premium whole life
20-year decreasing term
20-year level term life

explanation: Level term provides a fixed death benefit for a set period at a fixed premium with no cash value. It is the cheapest way to cover a temporary need such as raising children.

distractorExplanations.a: Whole life lasts for life and builds cash value, so its premium is much higher.
distractorExplanations.b: A single premium requires a large lump-sum payment up front.
distractorExplanations.c: Decreasing term reduces the death benefit over time, so it would not stay at $500,000.

Level premium whole life

Universal life

prompt: Hector named his sister as a revocable beneficiary and now wants his spouse to receive the proceeds instead. What does that change require?

A probate order, treating the designation as an amendment to his will
His written request to the insurer
Written consent from both his sister and his spouse before either name can change

explanation: A revocable beneficiary has an expectancy, not a vested right. The policyowner may change that designation without the beneficiary's consent by a written request to the insurer. An irrevocable beneficiary would have to consent before the change.

prompt: Using only the figures Devon wrote down, funeral costs are $8,000, the mortgage is $92,000, and income replacement is $300,000. He already holds $100,000 of group life coverage and $20,000 of savings he wants counted. How much additional insurance does the needs approach indicate?

$380,000, after subtracting the savings and leaving the group certificate in the gap
$120,000, the resources already on hand rather than the uncovered gap

explanation: The needs approach adds the stated needs and subtracts resources he already has. 8,000 + 92,000 + 300,000 = 400,000 of gross need. Group coverage of 100,000 plus savings of 20,000 equals 120,000. 400,000 - 120,000 = 280,000 of additional insurance.

distractorExplanations.b: Subtracts only the 20,000 of savings, since 400,000 - 20,000 = 380,000, and leaves out the 100,000 group certificate.
distractorExplanations.c: Reports the 100,000 + 20,000 = 120,000 of resources he already has instead of the uncovered gap.

prompt: Ignoring interest, Paula's human life value uses only these figures: she earns $60,000 a year, spends $15,000 a year on herself, and expects to work 20 more years. What amount does that method produce?

options.text: $1,200,000, from multiplying her full earnings by the years left, with personal spending left in
$300,000, from multiplying the amount she spends on herself by the years she plans to work
$45,000, one year of earnings after personal spending, with the 20 years left unused

explanation: Human life value here is family earnings after her own spending, over the years she expects to work, with interest ignored as stated. 60,000 - 15,000 = 45,000 a year. 45,000 × 20 = 900,000.

distractorExplanations.b: Forgets to remove personal spending: 60,000 × 20 = 1,200,000, which counts money she would have spent on herself.
distractorExplanations.c: Multiplies the wrong piece: 15,000 × 20 = 300,000 is her own spending, not the earnings the family loses.
distractorExplanations.d: Stops after 60,000 - 15,000 = 45,000 and never multiplies by the 20 years she expects to work.

prompt: A 42-year-old borrower compares policies for a mortgage that starts at $180,000 and will be $90,000 halfway through the term. Which policy's death benefit is built to fall with that balance?

options.text: Level term fixed at $180,000, which still pays the original amount when the loan is $90,000
Decreasing term from $180,000
Increasing term that starts lower than $180,000 and grows while the mortgage shrinks
Whole life with a level $180,000 face and cash value the lender did not ask for

explanation: Decreasing term starts at the original debt and declines over the term. Halfway, the stem's balance is 180,000 / 2 = 90,000, so a benefit that falls with the loan matches. Age 42 does not change that pattern. Level coverage would still pay 180,000 at the halfway point.

distractorExplanations.a: Keeps the death benefit at 180,000 when the loan has fallen to 90,000, so it does not track the balance.
distractorExplanations.c: Moves the death benefit the wrong direction: increasing term rises while this mortgage falls from 180,000 toward 90,000.
distractorExplanations.d: Uses permanent level coverage and cash value, while the debt itself declines from 180,000 to 90,000.

prompt: After several years in force, Greta asks why her level term policy still shows nothing she can borrow against. Which explanation is right?

Borrowing rights appear when the term renews, using the next premium as collateral for the loan
Term life builds no cash value
Level term pays a cash fund at the end of the level period if she is still living

explanation: Level term provides a death benefit for a stated period and does not accumulate cash value. Policy loans and surrenders come from the cash value of permanent insurance such as whole life. There is nothing in a level term policy for Greta to borrow.

distractorExplanations.a: Invents a hidden cash value and gives the beneficiary a loan right that term insurance does not create.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses renewal of term insurance with a cash-value loan. Renewal does not create collateral.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses level term with an endowment, which pays a living benefit if the insured survives the period.

prompt: A credit union may insure its borrower only to the extent of the debt owed to it. He owes this credit union $40,000 on one note and $15,000 on another. What maximum face amount does that insurable interest support?

$15,000, counting the smaller note and leaving out the first loan
$25,000, the difference between the two notes rather than the total owed

explanation: A creditor's insurable interest is limited to what the insured owes that creditor, and it must exist when the policy is issued. 40,000 + 15,000 = 55,000, so the face amount supported by this interest is $55,000.

distractorExplanations.a: Uses only the first note of 40,000 and ignores the additional 15,000 owed to the same creditor.
distractorExplanations.b: Uses only the smaller note of 15,000 and ignores the 40,000 balance on the other note.
distractorExplanations.c: Subtracts the loans, 40,000 - 15,000 = 25,000, instead of adding the debt that creates the interest.

distractorExplanations.b: Treats an irrevocable designation as revocable and skips the consent both the name change and the loan require.

distractorExplanations.d: Denies that the irrevocable beneficiary may consent. Her written consent is exactly what allows the change and the loan.

prompt: If the primary beneficiary dies before the insured, who is paid when the insured later dies and a secondary name is already on the policy?

The contingent beneficiary
The state unclaimed-property fund, because a predeceased primary cancels the claim
Whoever the primary beneficiary named in a personal will

Renewal without new evidence of insurability
A guaranteed insurability purchase that adds a separate block of coverage at stated dates

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses renewal of an in-force term contract with reinstatement, which follows a lapse and requires evidence of insurability.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses continuing the existing term with a guaranteed insurability rider that buys additional coverage.

Decreasing term, which pays a shrinking death benefit and never pays him for surviving

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses an endowment's face-amount payment with annuity income that is spread over his lifetime.
distractorExplanations.c: Uses decreasing term, which pays only a shrinking amount at death and nothing for survival.

prompt: A neighbor asks to own and pay for a policy on Sam's life and to name herself as beneficiary. She is not family and would lose no income if Sam died. What stops the insurer from issuing it?

prompt: When the insured dies with a living person named as beneficiary, which document decides who is paid the life insurance proceeds?

prompt: On this whole life contract the cash value is $25,000 and the face amount is $100,000. What net amount at risk remains with the insurer?

$25,000, the cash value alone, which is the savings already set aside rather than the risk

prompt: The needs worksheet already totals an income goal of $30,000 a year. The family wants to keep the principal intact and can earn 5% a year. How much capital does the capital retention method require?

distractorExplanations.b: Multiplies by the rate figure: 30,000 × 5 = 150,000, instead of dividing 30,000 by 0.05.

prompt: Camille converts her term policy to whole life and will not pay the extra sum that original-age conversion requires. She also takes no new medical exam. Which age sets the new premium?

prompt: Proceeds are payable to a minor child named as beneficiary, and no trust or adult custodian was arranged. What problem appears when the insured dies?

prompt: The designation reads children of the insured and lists no individual names. A child is born after the policy is issued and is alive when the insured dies. Who shares in the proceeds?

Every living child, including the later-born child
The oldest living child, paid as the sole representative of the class of children

explanation: A class designation such as children of the insured is determined at the insured's death. It includes class members then living, including a child born after issue. The owner does not have to amend the policy each time the class gains a member.

distractorExplanations.a: Freezes the class on the application date and excludes a child born later who is alive at death.
distractorExplanations.b: Requires a named endorsement. A class designation picks up a new member without listing that child.

prompt: Three children were named per capita. One child dies before the insured and leaves two offspring. The face amount is $300,000. How much does each surviving child receive?

$75,000, dividing the face among the two surviving children and the two offspring
$300,000, paying the entire face to each surviving child rather than splitting it

The deceased child's two offspring do not take that child's share. 3 named children minus the 1 who died leaves 3 - 1 = 2 survivors, so 300,000 / 2 = 150,000 each. Per stirpes would have passed the deceased child's share down that branch.

distractorExplanations.a: Still counts the deceased child: 300,000 / 3 = 100,000, instead of dividing by the 2 children who survived.

explanation: A collateral assignment gives the lender a security interest, not ownership of the policy. With the assignment on file, the insurer pays the bank the debt still owed, $18,000, and pays the rest of the $200,000 death benefit, $182,000, to the daughter. The bank does not take the full face amount, and a recorded collateral assignment is not ignored in favor of the beneficiary.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats a collateral assignment as an absolute transfer. The bank is paid only the $18,000 debt, not the entire $200,000 face amount.
distractorExplanations.b: Ignores an assignment the insurer has on file. The daughter does not receive the full $200,000 while $18,000 of recorded debt remains.
distractorExplanations.d: Swaps the lender's debt with the beneficiary's remainder. The bank receives the $18,000 still owed, and the daughter receives the other $182,000.

prompt: Yvonne signs an absolute assignment of her whole life policy to her adult son and notifies the insurer in writing. There is no irrevocable beneficiary. She later asks to rename the beneficiary and to take a policy loan. Who can exercise those rights?

options.text: Yvonne can, because an assignment never moves the right to rename the beneficiary or to borrow on the policy
The insurer can, because recording an assignment makes the company itself the new owner of the contract
The prior beneficiary can, because a beneficiary designation outranks an absolute assignment of ownership
Her son can, because the assignment gave him the owner's rights

explanation: An absolute assignment transfers every ownership right in the policy to the assignee. After Yvonne assigned the contract to her son and notified the insurer, he may change the beneficiary and request a policy loan. She no longer holds those rights. A collateral assignment would have secured a debt only. An irrevocable beneficiary, which this policy does not have, would have had to consent.

distractorExplanations.a: Leaves ownership with the assignor. An absolute assignment moves the rights to change the beneficiary and to borrow. Yvonne no longer has them.
distractorExplanations.b: Makes the insurer the owner because it recorded the form. Notice tells the company who the owner is. It does not make the company the owner.
distractorExplanations.c: Ranks a beneficiary above the owner. With no irrevocable beneficiary, the assignee-owner controls beneficiary changes and loans.

prompt: Jonah's life policy contains a spendthrift clause. After his death the insurer is holding the proceeds and paying them under a settlement option. A creditor of the beneficiary tries to garnish the funds still at the insurer. What does the clause do?

options.text: It blocks that creditor while the insurer still holds the funds
It pays the creditor ahead of the beneficiary and sends any leftover interest to the beneficiary later
It cancels the settlement option and forces an immediate lump sum into the creditor's hands
It lets the beneficiary pledge the unpaid installments as collateral for a new personal loan

explanation: A spendthrift clause protects death proceeds from the beneficiary's creditors while the insurer still holds them, and it generally stops the beneficiary from assigning or commuting those future payments. Jonah's clause therefore blocks the garnishment of funds still at the company. Money the beneficiary has already received can be reached like any other asset. The clause does not hand the proceeds to the creditor.

distractorExplanations.b: Reverses the clause and pays the creditor first. A spendthrift clause shields proceeds the insurer is still holding from the beneficiary's creditors.
distractorExplanations.c: Turns the settlement into a lump sum for the creditor. The clause keeps the funds at the insurer and blocks the garnishment. It does not redirect them.
distractorExplanations.d: Allows a pledge the clause is written to prevent. While the insurer holds the installments, the beneficiary generally cannot assign or borrow against them.

prompt: Nora's life policy names her brother as revocable beneficiary. She submits the insurer's signed change form and names a charity instead. Her brother refuses to agree. The policy says that completed form is all it requires. What is the result?

options.text: The change is refused, because a named beneficiary must consent before any new payee can be recorded
The charity replaces him, because his consent is not required
The charity is added beside her brother, because a new form keeps the revocable beneficiary and adds a second payee
The brother stays on the policy until the anniversary that follows the date on the change form

explanation: A revocable beneficiary has an expectancy, not a vested interest. The owner may name a new beneficiary without that person's consent. Nora completed the change form the policy requires, so the charity replaces her brother. Consent is required when the designation is irrevocable. The insurer does not hold the change until a later anniversary when the contract says the signed form is enough.

distractorExplanations.a: Requires consent that applies to an irrevocable beneficiary. Her brother is revocable, so his refusal does not block the change form.
distractorExplanations.c: Treats the change form as adding a second payee. A completed change of a revocable beneficiary replaces her brother, so the charity does not share the proceeds with him.
distractorExplanations.d: Delays the change until an anniversary the policy does not require. The contract says the completed form is enough, and Nora submitted it.

prompt: The beneficiary of a $240,000 death benefit asks the insurer to pay her $1,500 each month until the proceeds and interest run out. She does not pick a number of years. Which settlement option does she want?

options.text: Interest only, which pays earnings and leaves the $240,000 principal on deposit with the insurer
Fixed period, which starts by choosing the number of years and then calculates each installment from that term
Fixed amount, paying the chosen $1,500 until the fund is gone
A lump sum, which pays the entire $240,000 in one check during the first month of the claim

explanation: The fixed-amount settlement option lets the payee choose the installment size. The insurer pays $1,500 a month from the $240,000 proceeds plus interest until the fund is used up, so the number of months depends on the interest credited. A fixed-period option does the opposite: the years are chosen first and the payment is calculated. Interest only would not spend the principal.

distractorExplanations.a: Leaves the principal on deposit. She asked to receive $1,500 a month until the $240,000 fund and its interest are exhausted, which spends principal.
distractorExplanations.b: Chooses the length of time first. She did not pick a number of years. She picked a payment of $1,500, which is the fixed-amount option.
distractorExplanations.d: Pays the whole benefit at once. A lump sum would distribute the entire $240,000 now, not $1,500 a month.

prompt: Camille wants death-benefit payments she cannot outlive. If she dies early, she still wants those payments to continue until a minimum of 15 years has been paid. Which settlement option matches?

options.text: Interest only for 15 years, with the principal then paid in one sum to her estate
Fixed-amount installments that stop at the end of 15 years even if Camille is still living
Straight life income, which stops at her death and pays nothing further to any contingent payee
Life income with a 15-year period certain

explanation: Life income with a period certain pays Camille for as long as she lives. If she dies before the 15-year certain period is over, payments continue to a contingent payee until those 15 years are complete. Straight life income would stop at her death. Interest only does not promise an income she cannot outlive, and a fixed stop at 15 years could leave her unpaid if she lives longer.

distractorExplanations.a: Holds the principal and then pays it out. Interest only for 15 years does not guarantee income for the rest of her life if she lives past that point.
distractorExplanations.b: Stops at a fixed time even if she is alive. She asked for income she cannot outlive, plus at least 15 years of payments if she dies sooner.
distractorExplanations.c: Ends at her death with no further payments. Straight life income omits the 15-year guarantee she wants for a contingent payee.

prompt: A participating whole life illustration projects a dividend every year, and the policy says dividends are not guaranteed. The owner asks whether the insurer must pay next year's illustrated dividend. What should the agent answer?

options.text: No. Next year's illustrated dividend may be reduced or skipped
Yes. An illustrated dividend becomes a guaranteed payment for every later year of the contract
Yes, but only after the owner elects paid-up additions as the dividend option on the policy
No, unless the owner already has a policy loan large enough to secure next year's illustrated dividend

explanation: Dividends on a participating policy are a share of divisible surplus, and this contract says they are not guaranteed. An illustration is a projection, not an obligation, so the insurer may pay less than the pictured amount or pay no dividend next year. The dividend option controls how a declared dividend is applied. It does not force the company to declare one.

distractorExplanations.b: Turns a projection into a guarantee. The policy says dividends are not guaranteed, so next year's illustrated amount can be reduced or omitted.
distractorExplanations.c: Ties the guarantee to paid-up additions. That option only directs how a declared dividend is used. It does not require the company to declare one.
distractorExplanations.d: Links the dividend to a policy loan. A loan does not create a guaranteed dividend, and the illustration itself is not a promise.

prompt: Eli's participating whole life policy offers a dividend choice that buys one-year term insurance, in an amount equal to the policy cash value, and that extra term expires after the year. He selects it. Which dividend option is this?

options.text: Paid-up additions, which use the dividend as a single premium for small permanent policies that remain in force
One-year term, often called the fifth dividend option
Accumulation at interest, which leaves each dividend on deposit with the insurer so the deposit can earn interest
Reduction of premium, which applies the dividend to the next premium notice instead of buying any insurance

explanation: The one-year term dividend option uses a dividend to buy term insurance for one year, often in an amount equal to the cash value, and that term coverage ends when the year ends. It is often called the fifth dividend option. Paid-up additions buy permanent insurance that stays on the policy. Leaving the dividend at interest, or using it to reduce the premium, adds no term protection.

distractorExplanations.a: Buys permanent coverage instead of term. Paid-up additions remain in force. Eli's choice expires after one year and is tied to the cash value.
distractorExplanations.c: Leaves the dividend on deposit. Accumulation at interest earns interest on the dividend. It does not buy one-year term insurance.
distractorExplanations.d: Applies the dividend to the bill. Premium reduction lowers the next premium. It does not purchase term equal to the cash value.

prompt: Soren stops paying premiums on his whole life policy. He wants the company to send him the cash value and end the coverage. He does not want temporary term insurance or a smaller policy that stays in force for life. Which nonforfeiture option is he choosing?

options.text: Extended term, which keeps the full face amount in force for as long as the net cash value will pay for it
Reduced paid-up insurance, which buys a smaller permanent policy with no further premiums due from the owner
Cash surrender, which pays out the cash value and ends the coverage
An automatic premium loan, which borrows the unpaid premium from the cash value so the original policy does not lapse

explanation: Cash surrender is the nonforfeiture option that pays the owner the policy's cash value and terminates the insurance. Soren asked for the money and for coverage to end, so that option matches. Extended term keeps the full face amount for a limited time. Reduced paid-up keeps a smaller amount for life. An automatic premium loan pays a missed premium and does not surrender the contract.

distractorExplanations.a: Keeps the full face amount in force for a term. Soren does not want temporary insurance. He wants the cash value paid and the coverage ended.
distractorExplanations.b: Keeps a smaller policy in force for life. He said he does not want a paid-up policy. Cash surrender ends the insurance.
distractorExplanations.d: Uses the cash value to pay a premium and continue the original policy. An automatic premium loan is not a surrender, and coverage would not end.

prompt: Cash value in Priya's whole life policy is $8,200, and she has no policy loan outstanding. The contract limits any loan to the available cash value. She asks to borrow $12,000. What is the most the insurer can lend under that clause?

options.text: The full $12,000, because a life policy loan may exceed the cash value when the owner requests the larger amount
Nothing yet, because the cash value must grow from $8,200 to the $12,000 she requested before a loan is allowed
Nothing, because a loan is available only after the owner first surrenders the policy and ends the coverage
$8,200, the available cash value

explanation: A policy loan is secured by the cash value, and this contract will not lend more than the cash value available. With no loan outstanding, the most the insurer can lend Priya is $8,200, not the $12,000 she requested. She does not have to surrender the policy to borrow. Any later unpaid loan, and the interest charged on it, is deducted from the death benefit or the surrender value.

distractorExplanations.a: Lets the loan exceed the security. The clause caps the loan at the available cash value, so $12,000 is more than the $8,200 on hand.
distractorExplanations.b: Refuses any loan until the cash value equals the request. The clause allows a loan up to the cash value on hand, so the insurer can lend $8,200 now even though she asked for $12,000.
distractorExplanations.c: Requires a surrender before a loan. A policy loan borrows against cash value and leaves the contract in force. Surrender is a different option.

prompt: After delivery, an agent tells Luis that a scuba-diving exclusion will be removed if Luis agrees out loud. No company officer endorses the policy. Luis later dies while scuba diving, and the written exclusion is still in the contract. What controls the claim?

options.text: The written exclusion, because the policy was never endorsed
The agent's spoken promise, because a soliciting agent may delete an exclusion after the policy has been delivered
A waiver created by the first premium, because paying that premium erases every activity exclusion in the contract
The free-look provision, because that clause deletes hazardous-activity exclusions as soon as the policy is delivered to the owner

explanation: Under the entire-contract provision, the policy and the attached application are the agreement, and a change must be endorsed in writing by the company. The agent's oral statement does not remove the scuba-diving exclusion. Because that written exclusion is still in the contract, it controls the claim. Paying the first premium, and the free-look right, do not delete an exclusion the policy still contains.

distractorExplanations.b: Gives a soliciting agent power to rewrite the contract. An oral promise after delivery does not remove an exclusion. A company endorsement would be required.
distractorExplanations.c: Treats the first premium as a waiver of exclusions. Premium payment is consideration. It does not erase a scuba-diving exclusion that remains in the policy.
distractorExplanations.d: Uses the free look to delete exclusions. The free-look right is a limited time to return the policy. It does not cancel a written activity exclusion.

prompt: Amina's life policy is delivered with a 10-day free look printed on the first page. She returns the policy on day 7, asks for her money back, and has filed no claim. What refund does the free-look provision require?

options.text: Only the cash surrender value calculated on day 7, rather than the premium she paid to place the policy
The full premium she paid
Only the unused part of the premium, because a return on day 7 is a pro-rata cancellation of the 10-day free look
No refund, because the free look pays money only if the insured dies during those 10 days

explanation: The free-look provision in Amina's policy gives her 10 days from delivery to return the contract and receive a full refund of the premium. Day 7 is inside that period, and she has filed no claim. The refund is the premium she paid, not the cash surrender value and not a pro-rata share of the unused days. The free look is a buyer's reconsideration right, not a death benefit.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses the free look with a surrender. On day 7 of a 10-day free look the company refunds the premium, not the cash surrender value.
distractorExplanations.c: Treats the free look as a pro-rata cancellation. On day 7 of the 10-day free look the company refunds the full premium she paid, not only the unused days.
distractorExplanations.d: Turns the free look into a death benefit. The clause refunds premium if she returns the policy in time. It does not pay only if she dies.

prompt: Aisha's convertible term policy lets her switch it to whole life before age 60 with no medical exam. She is 47, still inside that deadline, and she applies to convert the same face amount. The new premium uses her age at conversion. What does the privilege provide?

options.text: Whole life at the premium charged on the day the term policy was originally issued to her
A larger face amount than the term policy, approved with no new underwriting of the increase
Whole life for the same face amount, with no exam, at her age-47 rate
A waiver of every future premium once the term coverage is changed over to whole life

explanation: A conversion privilege exchanges term coverage for permanent insurance without evidence of insurability when the owner converts before the deadline in the policy, here age 60. Aisha is 47, so she can move the same face amount to whole life with no medical exam. The new premium uses her attained age, 47, not the age when the term policy was issued. Conversion is not a guaranteed-insurability purchase of extra coverage, and it does not waive future premiums.

distractorExplanations.a: Keeps the original term premium. This policy prices the new whole life at the age at conversion, which is 47, not the age at issue.
distractorExplanations.b: Increases the face amount with no underwriting. That describes a guaranteed purchase option. Conversion here moves the same face amount.
distractorExplanations.d: Waives premiums at conversion. Changing term to whole life does not forgive future premiums. She pays the age-47 whole life rate.

prompt: Devin's individual health policy was issued with an exclusion rider for his left knee. He files one claim for surgery on that knee and another for a broken arm from a bicycle fall. The arm injury meets every other term of the policy. How do the two claims come out?

options.text: Both claims are denied, because an exclusion rider cancels the health policy from its original issue date
The knee surgery is paid and the broken arm is denied, because a rider reverses which benefits the policy covers
Both claims are paid, because a rider is only a note and cannot take away a benefit the policy lists
The arm can be paid, and the knee surgery is denied

explanation: An exclusion rider, also called an impairment rider, removes coverage for a condition named in the rider while the rest of the policy stays in force. Devin's rider names his left knee, so surgery on that knee is not a covered charge. The broken arm is a separate injury and can be paid because it meets the policy's other terms. The rider does not void the contract or reverse every other benefit.

distractorExplanations.a: Voids the whole policy because one condition is excluded. An exclusion rider limits the named knee condition. It does not cancel the contract from issue.
distractorExplanations.b: Reverses the rider's effect. The knee is the excluded condition, so that surgery is denied. The arm is a separate injury and can be paid.
distractorExplanations.c: Treats the rider as a note with no effect. An exclusion rider is part of the contract and removes coverage for the left knee.

prompt: Bea's disability income policy is guaranteed renewable to age 65. She has just filed a large claim, her premiums are current, and she fears the insurer will drop her or raise only her premium. What may the insurer do at the next renewal?

options.text: Raise the class rate, and still renew her policy
Cancel her policy at renewal because the new claim makes her an unacceptable single risk
Cut only her monthly benefit at renewal while leaving every other person in the class unchanged
Raise only her premium, because guaranteed renewable coverage reprices each person after a claim is filed

explanation: A guaranteed-renewable policy must be renewed up to the age stated in the contract as long as premiums are paid. Bea's policy runs to age 65, so the insurer cannot refuse her renewal or single her out for a benefit cut because of the claim. The company may raise the premium only by class. A noncancellable policy would also prevent that class increase. Canceling at renewal describes cancelable coverage.

distractorExplanations.b: Cancels at renewal because of one claim. Guaranteed renewable coverage to age 65 must be renewed while premiums are paid. One claim does not make it cancelable.
distractorExplanations.c: Cuts only Bea's monthly benefit. Guaranteed renewable coverage to age 65 cannot single her out for a smaller benefit at renewal. The insurer may raise the premium only for the whole class.
distractorExplanations.d: Reprices one insured after a claim. A guaranteed-renewable policy may raise rates for the class, not for Bea alone.

prompt: Lila applies to reinstate her lapsed individual health policy. Counting from the application, it reinstates on day 45 if the insurer has not refused. Accidents are covered at reinstatement. Sickness coverage begins 10 days after reinstatement. The insurer sends no reply. On day 50 she breaks a leg in an accidental fall. Influenza that started on day 48 is diagnosed that afternoon. Which loss is covered?

options.text: The broken leg and the influenza, because silence approves every loss that occurs after the application is signed
The broken leg only, because the influenza began inside the 10-day sickness wait
The influenza only, because sickness is covered sooner than an accidental injury once reinstatement is requested
Neither loss, because an unanswered reinstatement application keeps the lapsed policy from returning to force

explanation: The policy reinstates on day 45 because the insurer did not refuse. An accident is covered from that reinstatement, so the broken leg on day 50 is covered. Sickness coverage begins 10 days after reinstatement, so it is not available on day 48. The influenza started on day 48, only 3 days after day 45, and falls inside the 10-day wait. Silence after day 45 is not a denial under this clause.

distractorExplanations.a: Covers both losses from the application date. The contract reinstates on day 45, and sickness still waits 10 days. Influenza that started on day 48 is inside that wait.
distractorExplanations.c: Covers sickness ahead of accidents. This reinstatement does the reverse: the accidental leg injury on day 50 is covered, and the day-48 influenza is not.
distractorExplanations.d: Treats silence as a refusal. The policy says reinstatement occurs on day 45 if the insurer has not refused, and no refusal was sent.

prompt: Omar's life policy has a $60,000 face amount. The accidental-death rider adds another $60,000 only if death occurs within 90 days of an accident. He is injured in a crash and dies from those injuries on day 110. The base policy has no exclusion for this crash. What is payable?

options.text: $120,000, because the rider still adds its benefit when death follows the crash by more than 90 days
$60,000 from the rider alone, because a delayed accidental death replaces the base face amount
Nothing, because death on day 110 voids the base policy as well as the accidental-death rider
$60,000 from the base policy, because day 110 misses the rider limit

explanation: The accidental-death rider adds $60,000 only when death results from the accident within 90 days. Omar died on day 110, so the rider pays nothing. The base life policy still pays its $60,000 face amount, because the crash is not excluded there. Missing the 90-day limit does not void the base policy, and the rider does not replace that base benefit.

distractorExplanations.a: Pays the rider after the time limit. Day 110 is outside the 90-day accidental-death window, so the extra $60,000 is not added to the base.
distractorExplanations.b: Lets the rider replace the base policy. The rider pays nothing on day 110. The base policy still pays its own $60,000.
distractorExplanations.c: Voids the base policy because the rider's 90-day limit was missed. Day 110 eliminates only the extra $60,000. The base policy has no exclusion for this crash and still pays its own $60,000.

prompt: Which situation is a pure risk that can be insured?

options.text: The chance that a homeowner dies and leaves a mortgage unpaid
The chance of gaining or losing money on a stock purchase
The chance of winning or losing a bet on a football game
The chance of profit or loss from opening a new restaurant downtown

explanation: Pure risk offers only the chance of loss or no loss, never gain, so it is insurable. Speculative risk (investing, gambling, business ventures) involves a chance of gain and is generally not insurable.

distractorExplanations.b: Investing involves a chance of gain, which makes it speculative risk.
distractorExplanations.c: Gambling creates a chance of gain and is speculative, so it is uninsurable.
distractorExplanations.d: Business ventures can produce gains, so they are speculative risks.

prompt: A family buys life insurance so that the insurer, not the family, bears the financial loss if the breadwinner dies. Which risk management method is this?

options.text: Risk retention
Risk avoidance
Risk reduction
Risk transfer

explanation: Buying insurance is risk transfer: the financial consequences of a loss are shifted to the insurer in exchange for a premium. Avoidance, reduction, and retention are the other main methods.

distractorExplanations.a: Retention means the family would bear the loss itself.
distractorExplanations.b: Avoidance eliminates the activity that creates the risk.
distractorExplanations.c: Reduction lowers the chance or size of a loss, such as by quitting smoking.

prompt: After buying a disability policy, Jake starts taking fewer safety precautions at work because he knows he is covered. Which hazard does this describe?

options.text: Speculative hazard
Physical hazard
Morale hazard
Moral hazard

explanation: Morale hazard is indifference or carelessness because a person is insured. Moral hazard is dishonesty or bad character (for example fraud), and physical hazard is a physical condition that raises the chance of loss.

distractorExplanations.a: There is no 'speculative hazard'; speculative describes a type of risk.
distractorExplanations.b: A physical hazard is a tangible condition, such as a medical condition.
distractorExplanations.d: Moral hazard involves dishonesty, such as faking a claim, not carelessness.

prompt: Why does an insurer want to insure a large number of similar risks?

options.text: So it can avoid paying claims on unusual losses
So it can charge each insured a different premium that is unrelated to risk
So actual losses come closer to predicted losses (law of large numbers)
So every insured is guaranteed to have no losses in a given year

explanation: The law of large numbers says that as the number of similar exposure units grows, actual loss experience approaches expected loss. It lets insurers predict losses accurately and set fair premiums.

distractorExplanations.a: A larger pool makes losses predictable; it does not excuse paying claims.
distractorExplanations.b: Premiums are based on risk classes; large groups make those classes reliable.
distractorExplanations.d: Insurance cannot prevent losses; it spreads and predicts them.

prompt: People with serious health problems are more likely than healthy people to seek individual health coverage. What is this tendency called, and how do insurers control it?

options.text: Reinsurance, controlled by transferring risk to another insurer
Adverse selection, controlled through underwriting and enrollment rules
Moral hazard, controlled by increasing deductibles
Risk retention, controlled by having the employer self-insure the whole group

explanation: Adverse selection (anti-selection) is the tendency of higher-risk people to buy or keep insurance. Insurers control it through underwriting, waiting periods, participation requirements, and open enrollment windows.

distractorExplanations.a: Reinsurance shares an insurer's risk; it is not the tendency described.
distractorExplanations.c: Moral hazard concerns dishonesty after coverage; the issue here is who applies.
distractorExplanations.d: Retention is a risk management method, not the selection problem.

prompt: A life insurer issues a $20 million policy but keeps only $5 million of the risk, passing the rest to another insurer. What is this arrangement?

options.text: Coinsurance with the policyowner
A fraternal benefit arrangement
Risk avoidance
Reinsurance

explanation: Reinsurance transfers part of an insurer's risk (the ceding company) to another insurer (the reinsurer). It lets insurers write large policies while keeping losses within their retention limit.

distractorExplanations.a: Coinsurance shares health claims with the insured, not with another insurer.
distractorExplanations.b: Fraternal societies insure members; this is risk sharing between insurers.
distractorExplanations.c: The insurer still accepts the risk; it does not avoid it.

prompt: What does the applicant give as consideration in a life insurance contract?

options.text: The completed application and the initial premium
The agent's signature on the conditional premium receipt
The beneficiary's acceptance of the policy
The insurer's promise to pay the death benefit

explanation: A valid contract needs offer, acceptance, consideration, competent parties, and legal purpose. The applicant's consideration is the application plus the initial premium; the insurer's is its promise to pay covered claims.

distractorExplanations.b: The agent's receipt is not the applicant's consideration.
distractorExplanations.c: The beneficiary is not a party who gives consideration.
distractorExplanations.d: That is the insurer's consideration, not the applicant's.

prompt: An insured pays $800 in premiums and dies one month later, and the insurer pays a $250,000 death benefit. Which contract characteristic does this illustrate?

options.text: Conditional, because the insured must file a claim
Adhesion, because the insurer wrote the contract
Unilateral, because only the insurer makes a promise
Aleatory, because the exchange of values is unequal

explanation: Insurance is aleatory: the values exchanged are unequal and depend on an uncertain event. A small premium may produce a large benefit, or premiums may be paid for years with no claim.

distractorExplanations.a: Conditional refers to conditions the insured must meet, not the size of the exchange.
distractorExplanations.b: Adhesion concerns who drafted the contract, not unequal values.
distractorExplanations.c: Unilateral is true of insurance, but it does not explain the unequal exchange.

prompt: A court finds an ambiguous clause in a health policy and rules in favor of the insured. Which contract characteristic supports this ruling?

options.text: Contract of adhesion, so ambiguities are read against the insurer
Aleatory contract, so benefits are always paid in full
Utmost good faith, so the insured's reading of the clause controls
Unilateral contract, so only the insured may enforce it

explanation: Insurance policies are contracts of adhesion: the insurer drafts the terms and the applicant accepts them as written. Courts therefore resolve ambiguities in favor of the insured.

distractorExplanations.b: Aleatory refers to unequal exchange, not how ambiguity is interpreted.
distractorExplanations.c: Utmost good faith requires honesty from both parties; it is not this interpretation rule.
distractorExplanations.d: Unilateral means only the insurer makes a legally enforceable promise.

prompt: On her life insurance application, Jen states she exercises 'three times a week,' which is true to the best of her knowledge. How is this statement classified?

options.text: Concealment, because she did not attach exercise records
An estoppel, because the insurer relied on her statement
A representation, true to the best of her knowledge
A warranty, which must be literally true in every detail

explanation: Statements on life and health applications are representations: believed true to the best of the applicant's knowledge. A policy can be voided only if a misrepresentation is material. Warranties must be literally true.

distractorExplanations.a: Concealment is intentionally withholding material facts, not giving true answers.
distractorExplanations.b: Estoppel is a legal bar on an insurer reversing a position, not a type of statement.
distractorExplanations.d: Life and health application answers are generally treated as representations, not warranties.

prompt: An applicant knows he was recently diagnosed with cancer but does not mention it because the application did not ask directly. What is this called?

options.text: Concealment of a material fact
A breach of an express warranty
Waiver
Adverse selection

explanation: Concealment is intentionally withholding a material fact that would affect the insurer's decision. If proven, especially within the contestable period, it can allow the insurer to void the policy.

distractorExplanations.b: A warranty is a statement guaranteed to be true, not withheld information.
distractorExplanations.c: Waiver is an insurer voluntarily giving up a known right.
distractorExplanations.d: Adverse selection is a group tendency, not an individual act of withholding.

prompt: An agent's contract does not let him accept premiums after a policy lapses, but the insurer has regularly accepted late premiums he collected. A client reasonably believes he can accept them. What authority does the agent have in the client's eyes?

options.text: Fiduciary authority
Express authority
Apparent authority
Implied authority

explanation: Apparent (perceived) authority arises when an insurer's conduct leads a reasonable third party to believe the agent has authority. The insurer can be bound by acts within that apparent authority.

distractorExplanations.a: Fiduciary duty concerns handling client money; it is not a type of authority.
distractorExplanations.b: Express authority is what the agency contract grants in writing.
distractorExplanations.d: Implied authority covers actions needed to carry out express duties.

As an unauthorized insurer
As a domestic insurer
As an alien insurer

explanation: An insurer is domestic in its state of incorporation, foreign in other U.S. states, and alien if incorporated outside the U.S. An authorized (admitted) insurer holds a certificate of authority in the state.

distractorExplanations.b: Authorization depends on licensing, not on where it is incorporated.

A reciprocal exchange
A mutual insurer

distractorExplanations.a: Stock insurers are owned by shareholders, who receive taxable dividends.
distractorExplanations.b: Risk retention groups are liability insurers owned by members in one industry.
