prompt: Nora applies for a large life policy on herself and asks to name a local charity, which would lose nothing financially if she died, as beneficiary. She will own the policy. What insurable-interest rule decides whether that designation is allowed?

options.text: Nora has an unlimited interest in her own life and may name the charity despite its lack of a stake.
The charity must show it would lose income at her death, or naming it turns the policy into a wager.
Interest must still exist on the day she dies, so a charity that never depended on her cannot collect.
She may name the charity only if the charity buys the policy and becomes the owner at issue.

explanation: A person has an unlimited insurable interest in her own life, so Nora may insure herself and name any beneficiary, including a charity with no financial stake. The interest rule binds the owner when the policy is applied for. It does not require the payee to suffer a separate economic loss, and it does not have to be re-proved when she dies.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses the owner's interest with the beneficiary's. The charity does not need its own financial loss when Nora insures and owns the policy on her life.
distractorExplanations.c: Misstates the timing. Life insurance requires insurable interest at application, not at death, and Nora's interest in her own life meets that test.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses ownership with the beneficiary designation. Nora may own the policy on herself and still name a charity that does not buy it.

prompt: A credit union is owed 40,000 and applies to buy and own a 200,000 life policy on the borrower, with itself as beneficiary. There is no other debt or business tie. What insurable-interest limit applies to the credit union?

options.text: As a lender it has the same unlimited interest the borrower has in his own life, so any face amount is justified.
As the creditor, its interest is limited to the 40,000 debt, so 200,000 is more than that debt can support.
Written consent from the borrower removes the debt cap and lets the lender own any face amount.
The cap is the borrower's yearly wages, and the unpaid balance is irrelevant to the face amount.

explanation: A creditor's insurable interest in a debtor's life is limited to the debt and the charges tied to it. The credit union is owed 40,000, so owning 200,000 of coverage on the borrower gives it a payoff far beyond its loss. That excess is a wager. The borrower's consent does not enlarge the lender's interest, and his wages are not the measure.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses the borrower's unlimited interest in his own life with a creditor's interest. A lender that owns the policy is limited to the debt.
distractorExplanations.c: Treats consent as a substitute for insurable interest. Consent may be required, but it does not raise the lender's stake above the 40,000 debt.
distractorExplanations.d: Uses the wrong measure. A creditor's interest follows the debt, not the borrower's wages, so a 200,000 face amount is still excessive.

prompt: Investors with no family or business tie to Helen pay her a fee so she will apply for life insurance that they will own from the first day. She is insurable. Why should the carrier decline the case?

options.text: The fee makes Helen the true owner, so the investors' lack of a stake never has to be examined.
Interest is tested only when she dies, and the investors may acquire a stake years later.
They have no insurable interest when she applies, so the contract would be a wager on her death.
They are reinsurers of the issuing carrier, so they may own her new policy without an insurable interest of their own.

explanation: Life insurance requires an insurable interest when the policy is applied for. That interest is a close family tie or a real financial loss if the insured dies. Investors who will own the contract from inception, and who have neither tie, are betting on Helen's death. Her insurability and the fee do not create their interest, and the arrangement is not reinsurance.

distractorExplanations.a: Misreads the fee. Paying Helen to apply does not make her the owner when the investors are the owners from the first day, and it does not give them an interest.
distractorExplanations.b: Misstates the timing. Insurable interest in a life policy must exist at application, not only at death, so a stake the investors might gain later does not save the case.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a stranger-owned policy with reinsurance. Reinsurance is a carrier ceding risk to another carrier, not investors buying a policy on someone they will not lose money on.

prompt: A life applicant knows a recent diagnosis the carrier has not seen, and the carrier knows a coverage limit that does not appear in the papers given to the applicant. Each side is expected to reveal material facts the other cannot easily check. Which principle requires that honesty?

options.text: Adhesion, so any sentence the carrier drafted is read in the applicant's favor if the wording is unclear.
Aleatory exchange, so the applicant's payment and the benefit may fairly be unequal if a loss is uncertain.
Indemnity, so a life policy may pay only a measured economic loss and never a stated amount.
Utmost good faith, so each party must disclose the material facts the other has to rely on.

explanation: Insurance is a contract of utmost good faith. The applicant must disclose a material diagnosis the carrier has not seen, and the carrier must disclose a material coverage limit that was left out of the papers the applicant received. Each side holds facts the other must rely on and cannot cheaply verify. Adhesion, aleatory exchange, and indemnity answer different questions and do not create this mutual duty to speak.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses utmost good faith with adhesion. Adhesion is the rule for reading unclear carrier-drafted wording. It is not the duty to reveal facts the other party cannot see.
distractorExplanations.b: Names the wrong trait. An aleatory contract can exchange unequal values because loss is uncertain. That trait does not require disclosure of a hidden diagnosis or a hidden limit.
distractorExplanations.c: Misapplies indemnity. Life insurance is a valued contract that pays a stated amount. Indemnity is not the honesty principle described here.

prompt: On a life application, Andre writes that his last physical was about two years ago. He believes that. The visit was actually 26 months earlier. The carrier says the answer fails because it is not exact to the day. How should that statement be treated?

options.text: As a representation that is substantially true to the best of his knowledge, not exact to the day.
As a warranty, broken by any gap, so the policy is void even though the gap would not have changed the underwriting decision.
As concealment, because he did not attach the clinic record that shows the visit date.
As a waiver, because writing a time period gives up the carrier's right to ask for an exam.

explanation: Statements on a life application are representations. A representation must be true to the best of the applicant's knowledge and substantially correct, not exact in every detail. Andre's good-faith 'about two years' for a visit 26 months earlier meets that standard. The carrier may contest a representation only when it is false and material. Demanding literal exactness is the warranty rule, and it does not apply to this application answer.

distractorExplanations.b: Applies the warranty standard to an application answer. A warranty must be literally true. Andre's believed statement is a representation, so a small, good-faith gap is not automatically fatal.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a representation with concealment. Concealment is hiding a material fact. Andre answered the question with what he believed, and he was not required to attach the clinic record.
distractorExplanations.d: Misnames waiver. Waiver is a carrier voluntarily giving up a known right. An applicant's approximate date does not surrender the carrier's underwriting rights.

prompt: Two statements turn out slightly false, and neither fact would have changed the underwriting decision. One is an application answer the applicant believed. The other is a guarantee of exact truth written into the policy. Under the classic pairing, which statement can void the contract?

options.text: The believed application answer, because every representation voids the contract whether or not the fact would have changed the decision.
The exact-truth guarantee can void it, because a false warranty need not be material.
Neither statement, because both a representation and a warranty void coverage only when the applicant intended fraud.
Both statements, because a minor untruth cancels the policy for the same reason no matter which label it carries.

explanation: A representation is a statement believed true to the applicant's knowledge. It lets the carrier void the contract only when it is material, meaning the truth would have changed the decision. A warranty is a guarantee of literal truth built into the policy. Under the classic pairing, a false warranty can void the contract even when the point is not material. Here only the guarantee meets that test.

distractorExplanations.a: Reverses the materiality rule. An immaterial representation, including a believed application answer that would not have changed the decision, does not void the contract.
distractorExplanations.c: Adds an intent element the classic pairing does not require. A material misrepresentation or a broken warranty can void the contract without a separate finding that the applicant planned fraud.
distractorExplanations.d: Erases the difference. A representation and a warranty do not share the same materiality test, so a minor untruth does not automatically cancel both.

prompt: Many similar households each contribute to one life fund, and the death benefits of the few who die are paid from that shared fund. The description says nothing about forecasts becoming more accurate. Which idea does the fund illustrate?

options.text: The law of large numbers, because a shared fund is simply a promise that actual deaths will match a table.
Reinsurance, because each household shares the issuer's loss the way a reinsurer stands behind the company that issued the policies.
Risk pooling, in which the losses of the few are paid from contributions of the many.
Risk avoidance, because the households have eliminated the activity that creates the financial exposure.

explanation: Risk pooling puts many similar exposures into one fund so the contributions of the many pay the losses of the few. That is the sharing device inside insurance. The law of large numbers is a different idea: it is the reason a large pool's results become predictable. The households have not avoided the exposure, and they have not reinsured the carrier.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses pooling with the law of large numbers. The stem describes a fund that pays the few from the many. It does not describe actual results moving closer to a prediction.
distractorExplanations.b: Misnames reinsurance. Reinsurance is one carrier shifting risk to another carrier. Households contributing to a fund are not reinsuring the issuer.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses pooling with avoidance. Avoidance means not taking on the exposure. Paying into the fund spreads the financial loss. It does not mean the households dropped the activity that creates it.

prompt: An actuary compares deaths in a class of 40 similar, independent insureds with deaths in a class of 40,000 similar, independent insureds. In which class should actual deaths fall closer to the predicted rate, and why?

options.text: The class of 40, because a small group can be counted person by person and the prediction is then certain for every life.
Neither class, because this principle promises that every class will match its prediction with no remaining variance at all.
The class of 40,000 is less predictable, because a larger group creates more chances for a death the table did not name.
The class of 40,000, because actual results approach the expected rate as similar units grow.

explanation: The law of large numbers says that as the number of similar, independent exposure units grows, actual results move closer to the expected result. A class of 40,000 should track the predicted death rate more closely than a class of 40. The principle does not make any one death certain, and it does not wipe out variance. It makes the larger class more predictable, not less.

distractorExplanations.a: Reverses the size effect. A class of 40 is more likely to wander away from the predicted rate. Counting each person does not make the rate certain.
distractorExplanations.b: Overstates the principle. The law of large numbers says results tend toward the expectation as the class grows. It does not promise a perfect match or zero variance in a class of 40 or of 40,000.
distractorExplanations.c: Treats a larger class as noisier. Adding similar, independent insureds, from 40 to 40,000, pulls actual deaths toward the predicted rate instead of away from it.

prompt: A business owner asks a life and health carrier to cover injuries he plans to cause on purpose so he can file the claim and collect. The loss would have a clear dollar size. Why is that exposure not an insurable risk?

options.text: An insurable loss must be accidental and unintentional from the insured's side, not a planned act.
A clear dollar size is enough by itself, so a planned injury becomes insurable once the owner can state the amount.
Only speculative risks are insurable, and a planned claim is speculative, so the carrier should accept it.
Pooling this plan with other intentional claims makes the loss fortuitous, so the exposure then qualifies.

explanation: An insurable loss has to be fortuitous: accidental and outside the insured's deliberate control. Planning an injury in order to collect fails that test, even when the amount can be measured. A measurable size is necessary but not enough. Speculative risk is generally uninsurable too, and pooling intentional acts does not turn them into accidents.

distractorExplanations.b: Treats a measurable amount as the only test. A loss can have a clear size and still be uninsurable when the insured plans to cause it.
distractorExplanations.c: Reverses the risk types. Speculative risk, which can produce a gain, is generally not insurable. A planned injury also fails because it is not accidental.
distractorExplanations.d: Misuses pooling. Combining planned injuries does not make them fortuitous. Insurance pools accidental losses; it does not launder intentional ones.

prompt: A life claim file names a fatal heart attack as what produced the loss, and it names years of heavy smoking as the bodily condition that made that loss more likely. Which labels belong on those two facts?

options.text: Both facts are perils, because each one can be written on the claim as something that happened to the insured.
The heart attack is the peril that caused the loss, and the smoking is a physical hazard.
Smoking is the peril, and the heart attack is a morale hazard that appeared only because coverage was already in force.
Both facts are moral hazards, because the smoking and the heart attack show the insured planned the death and hid that plan.

explanation: A peril is the cause of the loss. On this file the peril is the fatal heart attack. A hazard is a condition that raises the chance or the size of a loss. Years of heavy smoking are a physical hazard because they are a bodily condition that made the peril more likely. Smoking is not the cause named in the claim, and a medical condition is not proof that the insured planned the death.

distractorExplanations.a: Collapses hazard into peril. A peril causes the loss. Smoking raised the chance of the heart attack, so it is a hazard, not a second cause of loss on this file.
distractorExplanations.c: Swaps the labels and the hazard type. The heart attack caused the loss, so it is the peril. Morale hazard is carelessness because coverage exists, not the heart attack itself.
distractorExplanations.d: Misuses moral hazard. Moral hazard is dishonesty, such as causing or faking a loss. A heart attack and years of smoking do not show that the insured planned the death or hid a plan to cause it.

prompt: Omar keeps his health policy. After a high blood-pressure reading he starts medicine and a daily walk so a stroke is less likely. Which risk-management method are the medicine and the walk?

options.text: Avoidance, because he ended the exposure that leads to a stroke, so the policy no longer has that loss to transfer.
Retention, because he has chosen to pay stroke costs himself and the policy no longer transfers that financial loss.
Reduction, which lowers the chance of loss while the health policy still transfers it.
Transfer, because the medicine and the daily walk shift the cost of a stroke from Omar to the health carrier.

explanation: Risk reduction, also called loss control, lowers how often a loss happens or how bad it is. Medicine and walking do that for stroke. Omar did not eliminate the exposure, and he kept the policy, so the remaining financial loss stays transferred. The medicine and the walk do not move that cost to the carrier, and they are not a decision to pay the stroke himself.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses reduction with avoidance. Avoidance means leaving the activity that creates the risk. Treatment lowers the chance of a stroke; it does not erase it.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses reduction with retention. Retention means bearing the financial loss. Omar kept the policy, so the medicine and the walk are not a decision to self-pay.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses reduction with transfer. The policy already transfers the financial loss. Medicine and walking only lower the chance of a stroke, and they do not shift that cost by themselves.

prompt: A health carrier's duty to pay arises only if a covered sickness occurs and the insured submits the proof the contract requires. If neither condition happens, the carrier pays nothing. Which contract trait do those facts show?

options.text: Aleatory, because the values exchanged can be unequal and depend on whether an uncertain loss happens to occur.
Unilateral, because only the carrier makes a legally enforceable promise and the insured does not promise to keep the policy.
Adhesion, because the insured had to take the carrier's wording as written and could not negotiate the clauses.
Conditional, because the carrier's duty to pay arises only when the required events occur.

explanation: A conditional contract makes the carrier's duty depend on events the policy names. Here the carrier pays only after a covered sickness and after the insured meets conditions such as proof of loss. If those events do not occur, nothing is owed. Aleatory refers to unequal, chance-based values. Unilateral means only the carrier promised. Adhesion refers to who wrote the form.

distractorExplanations.a: Describes a different trait. Aleatory means the values exchanged may be unequal because a loss may or may not occur. The stem is about duties that arise only when conditions are met.
distractorExplanations.b: Names unilateral form, not this fact pattern. Unilateral means only the carrier made an enforceable promise. It does not say the payment duty waits on a covered sickness and proof of loss.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses the trait with adhesion. Adhesion means the carrier drafted the form and the applicant accepted it as written. It does not describe when the duty to pay arises.

prompt: A producer leaves a health question blank, the applicant signs, and the carrier issues the policy knowing the answer is missing. Months later it denies a claim only because of that blank. Which doctrine names the carrier's voluntary giving up of the requirement?

options.text: Waiver, because issuing the policy voluntarily gave up a known right to that answer.
Estoppel, defined as the carrier's voluntary surrender of a right before anyone has relied on the issued policy.
A warranty, so the blank answer is guaranteed true and the claim has to be rewritten around that guarantee.
Apparent authority, because the producer who left the question blank had the power to waive that answer for the carrier.

explanation: Waiver is the voluntary relinquishment of a known right. By issuing the policy while it knew a question was blank, the carrier gives up the right to insist on that answer later. Estoppel is the related bar that stops the carrier from using the waived defect against someone who relied on the policy being issued. The blank is not a warranty, and the producer who skipped the question does not waive the carrier's right by doing so.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses waiver with estoppel. Estoppel is the legal bar after another party relies on the conduct. The voluntary giving up of a known right, which happened at issue, is waiver.
distractorExplanations.c: Mislabels the blank as a warranty. A warranty is a statement guaranteed to be literally true. An unanswered question is not a guarantee, and calling it one does not explain the carrier's giving up of the requirement.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses waiver with apparent authority. Apparent authority is what a third party may reasonably believe an agent can do. The producer skipping a question does not waive the carrier's right; issuing the policy with knowledge of the blank is the waiver.

prompt: Priya submits a life application together with the initial payment, and that package is her offer. The carrier will not take the requested rate class and instead issues a policy in a higher class. What must happen before a contract exists?

options.text: Nothing further. Issuing any policy, even on different terms, accepts her original offer as submitted.
Priya must accept the counteroffer, because the changed policy is not acceptance of her offer.
The producer must accept the higher class for Priya, because a producer binds both parties when a rated policy is issued.
Her initial payment accepts any policy the carrier issues, so the higher class binds her without a new acceptance.

explanation: The application plus the initial payment is the applicant's offer. If the carrier issues a policy on different terms, such as a higher rate class, that issue is a counteroffer rather than acceptance. No contract exists until Priya accepts the new terms. The producer cannot accept those terms for her, and the payment that came with her original offer does not accept a class the carrier had not yet offered.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats any issuance as acceptance. A policy issued on different terms is a counteroffer. It does not accept the offer Priya made.
distractorExplanations.c: Assigns acceptance to the wrong person. Priya is the applicant who must accept a counteroffer. A producer does not bind her to a higher rate class by accepting it for her.
distractorExplanations.d: Treats the original payment as acceptance of later terms. That payment was part of her offer. It cannot accept a higher rate class the carrier had not yet offered.

prompt: Cole receives a client's initial life-policy payment and is told to keep that money apart from his own funds and to forward it promptly to the carrier. Which duty requires that handling?

options.text: Apparent authority, because a client who sees him take the premium may believe he can keep that money with his own funds.
Waiver, because taking the money gives up the carrier's right to investigate the risk before issue.
A fiduciary duty to hold the client's and the company's money in trust and send it on.
Utmost good faith, because the duty to disclose medical facts on the application is also what requires him to segregate and forward the premium.

explanation: A producer who handles a client's payment is a fiduciary. The money belongs to the client or the carrier, so it must stay separate from personal funds and be forwarded as the appointment requires. That is a trust duty about other people's money. It is not the authority a client may think the producer has, and it is not a waiver of underwriting. It is also not the duty to disclose medical facts.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a fiduciary duty with apparent authority. Apparent authority is what a third party may reasonably believe the producer can do. It does not require him to keep client money separate from his own funds and forward it.
distractorExplanations.b: Misnames waiver. Waiver is giving up a known right. Receiving and forwarding a payment does not surrender the carrier's right to underwrite the risk.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a fiduciary duty with utmost good faith. Utmost good faith is the duty to disclose material facts. It is not the duty to segregate a client's premium and forward it to the carrier.

prompt: One carrier insures only the night-shift workers at a single plant. One explosion could kill many of them in the same event. Why does the law of large numbers give this book little help?

options.text: The principle applies only to health claims, so a life exposure is outside its scope however the deaths occur.
Hiring a larger shift at that same plant would make the results less reliable, because the principle works only for tiny groups.
Workplace deaths are speculative risk, so the law of large numbers cannot produce a reliable average for this group of workers.
The lives are not independent, so one event can cause many losses at the same time.

explanation: The law of large numbers needs a large number of similar exposures whose losses are independent, so high and low results can cancel. If one explosion can kill many insured workers together, the losses move as a group and will not settle near the average. That is a correlated, catastrophic exposure. Putting more workers in the same plant would not make those lives independent.

distractorExplanations.a: Limits the principle to health claims. The law of large numbers is used for life exposures too. The problem on this book is dependence, not the line of business.
distractorExplanations.b: Reverses how group size works and misses the defect in the stem. A larger group helps only when losses are independent. More workers at the same plant would still share one explosion.
distractorExplanations.c: Misclassifies the risk. Death is a pure risk of loss with no chance of gain, not a speculative risk. The principle fails here because one explosion can kill many insureds together, not because death is speculative.

prompt: A healthy 66-year-old worries that she will outlive her retirement savings. Which risk does a life annuity primarily protect against?

options.text: Mortality risk, by paying her heirs if she dies early
Inflation risk, by guaranteeing payments that rise with prices
Market risk, by guaranteeing returns in a variable account
Longevity risk, by paying income for as long as she lives

explanation: Life insurance protects against dying too soon; a life annuity protects against living too long. It pools longevity risk and guarantees income for life, however long the annuitant lives.

distractorExplanations.a: Protection against dying too soon is the role of life insurance, not a life annuity.
distractorExplanations.b: Most fixed life annuities pay level amounts unless an inflation rider is added.
distractorExplanations.c: Variable accounts carry market risk; the life annuity's core role is lifetime income.

The free-look phase
The accumulation phase
The elimination phase

explanation: During the accumulation (pay-in) phase, the owner pays premiums and earnings grow tax-deferred. In the annuitization (payout) phase, the value is converted into a stream of income payments.

distractorExplanations.a: Annuitization is the payout phase when income payments begin.

options.text: A variable deferred annuity
A level term life policy
A flexible premium deferred annuity
A single premium immediate annuity

explanation: An immediate annuity is bought with a single premium and begins payments within 12 months, often one month after purchase. Deferred annuities accumulate value before payments start later.

distractorExplanations.b: Life insurance protects against early death, not outliving income.

prompt: Which feature describes a fixed annuity?

options.text: The insurer guarantees principal and a minimum interest rate
The annuity pays only if the insured dies during the term
The owner chooses subaccounts and bears investment risk
Payments rise and fall with a stock index without any floor or cap

explanation: A fixed annuity's assets are in the insurer's general account. The insurer bears the investment risk and guarantees principal and a minimum interest rate, so payments are level and predictable.

distractorExplanations.b: A death-only payment describes term life insurance, not an annuity.

Accumulation units
Annuity units
Paid-up additions

The Consumer Price Index, adjusted every year
The value of each annuity unit, which tracks the separate account

explanation: The number of annuity units is fixed at annuitization, but each unit's value changes with the separate account's performance, so variable annuity payments rise or fall.

prompt: A fixed indexed annuity has 80% participation, an 8% cap, and a 0% floor. The index gains 12% this year. What interest is credited?

distractorExplanations.a: The floor applies only when the index is flat or negative.
distractorExplanations.c: This is 80% of the 12% gain before the cap is applied.
distractorExplanations.d: Credits the full index gain, ignoring the participation rate and cap.

prompt: A retiree wants the highest possible monthly annuity income for his own life and does not care about leaving money to heirs. Which payout option fits?

options.text: Life with 10-year period certain
Straight life (life only)
Cash refund life annuity
Joint and 100% survivor

prompt: After years of paying into a deferred annuity, Omar converts the account to monthly income that will last for his life. Which phase is the contract in now?

options.text: The accumulation phase, because the insurer is still collecting premiums while income is paid

The free-look phase, because starting lifetime income reopens the delivery review
The elimination phase, because lifetime income is a waiting period before benefits

explanation: Accumulation is the pay-in phase, when premiums grow tax-deferred. Omar has stopped paying in and has converted the account to lifetime income, so the contract is now in the payout, or annuitization, phase.

prompt: Lena's deferred annuity has an account value of $40,000. Her contract states a 5% surrender charge on a full surrender of that value, and no free-withdrawal amount remains. Ignoring taxes, what does she receive?

$36,000, after a second penalty that her contract does not state

explanation: Surrender charge = 5% × $40,000 = $2,000. Amount she receives = $40,000 − $2,000 = $38,000. The only charge used is the 5% stated for this surrender, and taxes are left out as the question directs.

distractorExplanations.a: Mistake: ignores the 5% charge stated for this surrender and pays her the full $40,000 as if the charge began only after annuitization.
distractorExplanations.b: Mistake: pays her the $2,000 charge itself. That amount is subtracted from the $40,000, not handed to her as the proceeds.

explanation: A fixed annuity's assets sit in the insurer's general account. The insurer bears the investment risk and must support the principal promise even if its own investments earn less. That is the opposite of a variable annuity, where the owner bears separate-account risk.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a fixed annuity with a variable annuity. On the fixed contract, Marcus does not absorb the insurer's investment losses.
distractorExplanations.b: Misassigns the risk to the beneficiary. The insurer carries the investment risk while this fixed annuity is in force.

explanation: An immediate annuity starts income within 12 months of the premium. Noah waits 6 years, and 6 × 12 = 72 months. Because 72 is greater than 12, the contract is deferred. A single premium can fund either form; the start date is what decides.

distractorExplanations.b: Mistake: treats a single premium as a one-month start. His income waits 6 × 12 = 72 months, so the annuity is deferred.

distractorExplanations.c: Mistake: selects the taxable slice. $6,000 − $2,400 = $3,600 is earnings, not the amount the exclusion ratio removes from income.
distractorExplanations.d: Mistake: excludes the whole $48,000 investment from a single year. The ratio spreads that investment over the $120,000 expected return.

prompt: Evan wants to move the $70,000 cash value of his life policy, which has a $40,000 cost basis, into an annuity without recognizing the gain now. Which transfer does that?

distractorExplanations.b: Mistake: reverses the allowed direction. An annuity-to-life move is not a tax-free 1035 exchange; life-to-annuity is.

prompt: Grace owns an annuity on her own life and has named her brother as beneficiary. While the contract is still in accumulation, who may change that beneficiary or surrender it?

prompt: Andre's account value is $50,000. The contract allows a 10% free withdrawal this year and then an 8% surrender charge on any amount above that. He withdraws $9,000. What charge applies?

distractorExplanations.b: Mistake: charges 8% × $9,000 = $720 on the whole withdrawal and skips the $5,000 free amount the contract allows.
distractorExplanations.c: Mistake: treats the $5,000 free withdrawal as the charge. That slice is the part he can take with no surrender charge.
distractorExplanations.d: Mistake: calls the $4,000 excess the charge. The charge is 8% of that excess, and 8% × $4,000 = $320.

prompt: June's fixed indexed annuity states a 0% floor. The linked index falls 9% this year. How much interest is credited, and who bears the loss below that floor?

explanation: The floor is 0%, and 0 is greater than −9, so credited interest is 0% rather than −9%. The gap not passed through is 0 − (−9) = 9 percentage points, and the insurer bears that downside. This is not a separate-account variable annuity.

distractorExplanations.a: Mistake: treats the contract as a variable annuity and credits the −9% index loss to June. The stated floor stops the credit at 0%.

prompt: Nora's deferred annuity applies a market-value adjustment that compares the 3% rate set at issue with a 5% rate used on surrender. Rates have risen. What does the adjustment do to her cash surrender value?

prompt: Priya, an agency employee, quotes life premiums, compares policies, and asks clients to sign applications. A coworker in the same office only files completed forms and never discusses coverage. Who must hold a producer license?

options.text: Priya, because she quotes premiums and takes applications
The coworker who files forms, because paperwork is the act the license covers
Neither employee, because the insurer's appointment of the agency covers the staff
Both employees, because working inside the agency office is itself solicitation

explanation: Anyone who sells, solicits, or negotiates insurance must hold a producer license. Quoting premiums, comparing policies, and asking for an application is soliciting, so Priya must be licensed. Filing completed forms without discussing coverage is clerical work and does not by itself require a license. An insurer's appointment of the agency does not license the staff.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses filing with soliciting. The coworker never discusses coverage, so the license duty falls on Priya, not on the person who files forms.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses an appointment with a license. An appointment lets a licensed producer represent an insurer; it does not authorize unlicensed employees to solicit.
distractorExplanations.d: Treats office presence as solicitation. A license is required for selling, soliciting, or negotiating, not for merely working in the building.

prompt: On a sales call, the producer tells a prospect that dividend projections in a whole life illustration are guaranteed benefits. The policy says dividends are not guaranteed, and no existing policy is being replaced. Which unfair practice is this?

options.text: Twisting, because a talk about dividends is treated as replacing another policy
Misrepresentation of the policy terms
Rebating, because labeling a dividend guaranteed offers value the contract omits
Defamation of the company that produced the sales illustration

explanation: Misrepresentation includes a false statement of policy terms, benefits, or dividends. Illustrated dividends are not guaranteed, so calling them guaranteed benefits misstates the contract the client would buy. The call does not describe a replacement, a payment of value outside the policy, or a false attack on another company's reputation.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses this false statement with twisting. Twisting uses misrepresentation to induce a client to drop an existing policy, and no replacement is described here.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a false description with rebating. Rebating is offering value the policy does not provide, not mislabeling a dividend projection as guaranteed.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a statement to the buyer with defamation. Defamation is a false remark that injures an insurer's reputation, which this dividend claim does not do.

prompt: Nora owns a non-MEC universal life policy. She has paid $24,000 in premiums, cash value is $31,000, and she withdraws $5,000. The same week a policy on her uncle pays her a $100,000 lump-sum death benefit. How is each amount taxed as income?

options.text: The withdrawal is ordinary income and the death benefit is ordinary income
The withdrawal is tax-free, while $7,000 of the death benefit is ordinary income
Withdrawal recovers basis tax-free, and the death benefit is excluded
The withdrawal and the death benefit are both taxed as long-term capital gain

explanation: A non-MEC life withdrawal is basis-first. Gain inside Nora's contract is $31,000 - $24,000 = $7,000, but the $5,000 withdrawal does not exceed her $24,000 basis, so taxable income on the withdrawal is $0. Basis left is $24,000 - $5,000 = $19,000. The $100,000 lump-sum death benefit is excluded from income, so its taxable amount is $0 as well.

distractorExplanations.a: Taxes both receipts as ordinary income. The $5,000 comes out of the $24,000 basis first, and a lump-sum life death benefit is excluded from income.
distractorExplanations.b: Moves the $7,000 cash-value gain onto the death benefit. That $7,000 stays inside Nora's contract, and the uncle's $100,000 proceeds are excluded.
distractorExplanations.d: Labels both amounts capital gain. A non-MEC withdrawal above basis would be ordinary income, this $5,000 is not above basis, and death proceeds are excluded.

prompt: Helen has kept a life policy in force for 9 years, past its 2-year contestable period, and the suicide period on that policy has expired. She applies for a new life policy and will lapse the old one at delivery. The producer completes the replacement forms. What new exposure does the replacement create?

options.text: No added exposure, since signed replacement forms erase the contestable period in the new contract
A new contestable period when the producer gives a false description of the old policy
Forfeiture of the old policy's cash value on the application date, before the new contract is delivered
New contestable and suicide periods on the policy purchased

explanation: A replacement starts the new policy's contestable period and suicide period even when the forms are completed honestly. Helen's old policy has been in force 9 - 2 = 7 years beyond its contestable period, and that suicide period has already ended. The new contract opens those periods again. The forms disclose the replacement; they do not waive it. The old policy should stay in force until the new one is delivered.

distractorExplanations.a: Thinks the replacement forms waive contestability. Those forms document the change; they do not erase the new policy's contestable period.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a proper replacement with twisting. The new contestable and suicide periods apply even when the producer describes the old policy truthfully.
distractorExplanations.c: Treats the application date as a surrender. She can keep the old policy, including its cash value, until the new policy is delivered.

prompt: Marco collects a $420 initial life premium from an applicant on Monday and deposits that $420 in his personal checking account, planning to send it to the insurer on Friday. Which duty has he broken?

options.text: Keeping client premium money out of his personal account
Quoting a premium below the $420 the insurer charged for this policy
Sending a replacement notice, because every first premium starts a replacement
Avoiding a rebate, because parking the premium in his account returns $420 to the client

explanation: Premium funds are held in a fiduciary capacity and must stay separate from personal money. Marco received $420 and has forwarded $0, so $420 - $0 = $420 of the applicant's premium is sitting in his personal account. Planning to remit the full $420 on Friday does not undo the commingling.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses commingling with charging less than the stated premium. He collected the $420; the broken duty is placing that $420 in his personal account.
distractorExplanations.c: Treats every new premium as a replacement. Replacement involves existing coverage being dropped or used to fund new coverage, which this deposit does not show.
distractorExplanations.d: Calls the deposit a rebate to the client. The $420 remains premium owed to the insurer, and a rebate would be value returned to the applicant as an inducement.

prompt: To close a health sale, a licensed producer offers the applicant $300 of the commission if she applies today. Nothing in the policy pays her that $300. What is this offer?

options.text: A permitted price cut, because any producer may hand commission dollars back to a buyer
Rebating value the policy itself does not pay
Twisting, because paying part of the commission shows that an old policy is being replaced
A Fair Credit Reporting Act disclosure required before the policy can be delivered

explanation: Rebating is offering the applicant an inducement of value that the policy does not provide. The producer offered $300 of commission, and the contract pays $0 of that amount, so the inducement is $300 - $0 = $300. The offer is not a notice about a consumer report, and it does not describe replacing an existing policy.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats a commission kickback as an ordinary discount. Returning $300 that the policy does not pay is an inducement, not a reduction of the filed premium.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses rebating with twisting. Twisting misleads a client into replacing a policy, and this offer does not mention existing coverage.
distractorExplanations.d: Assigns the payment to the Fair Credit Reporting Act. That law covers consumer reports used in underwriting, not a $300 commission offer to the applicant.

prompt: Owen has paid $8,000 of premiums on a participating whole life policy. Cash dividends from earlier years total $7,500. This year the insurer pays a $1,200 cash dividend. None of the dividends bought paid-up additions. How much of this year's dividend is taxable income?

options.text: $0 of this year's dividend
$500 of this year's dividend
$700 of this year's dividend
$1,200 of this year's dividend, plus the $7,500 already received

explanation: Cash dividends on a life policy are a return of premium until they exceed basis, and any excess is ordinary income. Remaining basis before this dividend is $8,000 - $7,500 = $500. Of the $1,200 dividend, $500 is tax-free and $1,200 - $500 = $700 is taxable. The earlier $7,500 was already applied against basis and is not taxed again.

distractorExplanations.a: Stops at the idea that dividends are tax-free and skips the basis limit. After $7,500 of the $8,000 basis is used, $1,200 - $500 = $700 of this dividend is income.
distractorExplanations.b: Reports the remaining basis as the tax. The $500 is the tax-free slice of this dividend; the taxable slice is $1,200 - $500 = $700.
distractorExplanations.d: Taxes the entire $1,200 and the prior $7,500 again. Prior dividends already reduced basis, and $500 of this year's dividend is still a nontaxable return of premium.

prompt: Rita purchases an existing life policy on her neighbor from the neighbor for $10,000. She pays $4,000 of later premiums. When the neighbor dies, the insurer pays Rita $50,000. No transfer-for-value exception applies. How much of the $50,000 is taxable income to Rita?

options.text: $0, since the death payment is excluded from Rita's gross income
$4,000, matching the premiums she paid after the purchase
$14,000, matching her purchase price plus the later premiums
$36,000, the proceeds left after her basis is removed

explanation: A transfer for value makes death proceeds taxable to the extent they exceed the buyer's consideration plus later premiums, unless an exception applies. Rita's basis is $10,000 + $4,000 = $14,000. Taxable income is $50,000 - $14,000 = $36,000. A purchase from a neighbor is not a transfer to the insured, a partner, a partnership, or a corporation in which the insured is a shareholder or officer.

distractorExplanations.a: Applies the ordinary death-benefit exclusion. A transfer for valuable consideration blocks that exclusion when no statutory exception applies, so the gain is taxed.
distractorExplanations.b: Counts only the $4,000 paid after the purchase. Basis also includes the $10,000 price, and the taxable gain is $50,000 - $14,000 = $36,000.
distractorExplanations.c: Stops at basis and reports $14,000 as the tax. That $14,000 is recovered tax-free; income is $50,000 - $14,000 = $36,000.

prompt: Kim's individually owned medical policy, with premiums she paid herself, reimburses her $2,400 for a covered surgery. The payment matches the surgical bill, and no employer paid the premium. How much of the $2,400 is included in her income?

options.text: $0 of the reimbursement
$2,400, on the ground that she paid these premiums herself
Whatever part of the $2,400 exceeds the premiums she paid this year
$2,400, reported as a long-term capital gain from the policy

explanation: When the insured paid the medical premiums, insurance that reimburses medical expenses is excluded from income. The payment equals the surgical bill, so the taxable portion is $2,400 - $2,400 = $0. Paying the premium herself does not turn the reimbursement into wages or into capital gain.

distractorExplanations.b: Treats self-paid premiums as a reason to tax the benefit. Those premiums are why the $2,400 reimbursement is excluded, and the taxable amount is $0.
distractorExplanations.c: Imports a life-insurance basis formula into a medical reimbursement. This $2,400 matches a medical bill, so there is no premium-excess gain to compute.
distractorExplanations.d: Calls the reimbursement a capital gain. Medical benefits are not capital transactions, and this $2,400 is excluded from income.

prompt: A licensed life producer wants to pay an unlicensed friend part of the commission. The friend quoted the premium and joined the meeting where the buyer decided to apply. May the producer share that commission?

options.text: Yes, provided the licensed producer is the one who signs the application
No, the friend solicited the sale without a producer license
Yes, licensed producers may split commissions with anyone who helped the sale
No, unless the friend is moved onto the insurer's payroll before the meeting

explanation: A person who quotes coverage and helps a buyer decide to apply is soliciting and must be licensed for that line. Commission for the sale may be shared with another licensed producer, not with an unlicensed friend who negotiated the sale. Who signs the form, or a later place on payroll, does not erase the unlicensed solicitation.

distractorExplanations.a: Thinks the signature is the licensed act. Quoting the premium and helping the buyer decide is soliciting, even when a licensed producer signs the form.
distractorExplanations.c: Allows a commission split with any helper. An unlicensed person who solicits may not be paid commission for that sale.
distractorExplanations.d: Substitutes a payroll status for a license. Salary does not authorize an unlicensed person to quote coverage and help close the sale.

prompt: Worried that a prospect distrusts a small life insurer, the producer describes the state life and health guaranty association and says its protection is a reason to buy the policy. What is wrong with using the association that way?

options.text: Nothing is wrong, because life sales presentations must describe that protection
The producer was required to promise the dollar amount the association would pay
That protection may not be used to induce the purchase
The comment is misplaced because guaranty associations exist for homeowners policies

explanation: State life and health guaranty associations give limited protection if a member insurer becomes insolvent, but producers must not use the association to induce someone to buy. Describing that protection as a reason to purchase violates the rule. The pitch also should not promise a payout figure, and this association is not a homeowners program.

distractorExplanations.a: Reverses the sales rule. Mentioning the association to encourage a purchase is prohibited, not a required part of the presentation.
distractorExplanations.b: Adds a dollar promise the producer must not make. The violation is using the association as an inducement, and no payout figure belongs in the pitch.
distractorExplanations.d: Moves the association to homeowners coverage. A life and health guaranty association relates to life and health insurers, and it still cannot be used to close this sale.

prompt: While a life application is still pending, the producer tells relatives at dinner the applicant's name and the heart condition listed on the medical records. Which duty did the producer violate?

options.text: A replacement duty to pass those medical details to the previous insurer
A McCarran-Ferguson duty to announce the diagnosis to state officials
The rebating rule, because describing the condition gives the family something of value
Confidentiality of the applicant's medical information

explanation: Producers must keep an applicant's nonpublic medical information confidential and use it for the insurance purpose that required it. Naming the applicant and describing the heart condition at dinner is an unauthorized disclosure. Replacement notices, the McCarran-Ferguson Act, and rebating rules do not ask for or excuse that disclosure.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses privacy with replacement. Medical details are not a dinner topic for a prior insurer, and the stem does not describe a replacement at all.
distractorExplanations.b: Assigns the disclosure to the McCarran-Ferguson Act. That act leaves insurance regulation with the states; it does not tell a producer to reveal a diagnosis.
distractorExplanations.c: Calls the disclosure a rebate. A rebate is value offered to induce a purchase, not an unauthorized description of an applicant's medical facts.

prompt: Imani owns a non-MEC whole life policy. Premiums paid are $18,000 and the cash value is $26,000. She borrows $3,000 from the cash value and does not surrender or lapse the policy. How much of the $3,000 loan is taxable income this year?

options.text: $3,000 is ordinary income, taxed as gain before any basis
The $8,000 gain is income now, even though she borrowed less than that
She has a $15,000 capital loss, equal to premiums paid minus this loan
None of the $3,000 is taxable income this year

explanation: A loan from a non-MEC life policy is not a current distribution. The contract holds $26,000 - $18,000 = $8,000 of unrealized gain, but borrowing $3,000 does not recognize it, so taxable income on the loan is $0. Subtracting the loan from premiums, $18,000 - $3,000 = $15,000, is not a capital loss. Gain-first taxation applies to a MEC loan, and this policy is not a MEC.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats a non-MEC loan as a gain-first distribution. That treatment fits a loan from a MEC; this $3,000 loan is not currently taxable.
distractorExplanations.b: Taxes unrealized gain. The $8,000 gain stays in the contract, and a non-MEC loan does not pull it into this year's income.
distractorExplanations.c: Invents a capital loss. Premiums are basis, and $18,000 - $3,000 is not a deductible loss created by taking a policy loan.

prompt: Nia's employer pays $3,600 this year for her group health coverage, and Nia pays the other $1,200 from after-tax wages. Nia is an employee, not a partner and not an S corporation shareholder. How much of the employer's $3,600 is included in her gross income?

options.text: $4,800, adding her payroll share to the employer's payment
$1,200, the portion that came out of her own wages
$3,600 as taxable wages, because an employer payment for health coverage is income
$0 of the amount her employer paid

explanation: Employer payments for an employee's group health coverage are excluded from the employee's gross income. Nia is not a partner or an S corporation shareholder, so the included amount of the employer payment is $3,600 - $3,600 = $0. Her own $1,200 is premium she paid, not pay she received. Adding the two shares would count $1,200 + $3,600 = $4,800 she did not receive as wages.

distractorExplanations.a: Adds her $1,200 premium to the employer's $3,600 and calls the $4,800 income. She did not receive her own premium as wages, and the employer share is excluded.
distractorExplanations.b: Taxes the share she paid herself. The $1,200 came from after-tax wages; the amount asked about is the employer's $3,600, which is excluded.
distractorExplanations.c: Includes the employer payment as wages. Group health premiums an employer pays for an employee are excluded, so the included amount is $0.

prompt: A surgeon wants disability coverage that pays if she cannot perform surgery, even if she could teach medicine instead. Which definition of total disability fits?

options.text: Any occupation
Presumptive disability
Partial disability
Own occupation

explanation: An own-occupation definition pays benefits when the insured cannot perform the material duties of her own occupation, even if she works elsewhere. Any-occupation definitions are stricter and cheaper.

distractorExplanations.a: Any occupation pays only if she cannot work in any job suited to her training.
distractorExplanations.b: Presumptive disability covers specific severe losses such as blindness.
distractorExplanations.c: Partial disability covers inability to perform some duties, not total disability.

The maximum length of time benefits will be paid
The time before a pre-existing condition is covered
The time after disability starts before benefits begin

distractorExplanations.a: Contesting misstatements falls under the time limit on certain defenses.
distractorExplanations.b: That is the benefit period, here 5 years.

He receives a partial benefit because he can still earn income
He receives benefits only if he cannot do any job
He is considered totally disabled even if he could still work

explanation: Presumptive disability provisions treat specified severe losses (sight, hearing, speech, or use of two limbs) as total disability, paying full benefits even if the insured returns to work.

distractorExplanations.b: Presumptive disability pays full benefits regardless of earnings.

prompt: Before disability, Amir earned $10,000 a month. After a heart attack he returns to work part-time earning $4,000 a month. His policy's full benefit is $5,000 a month and includes a residual disability benefit. What does he receive?

$3,000 a month
$5,000 a month
$6,000 a month

distractorExplanations.c: The full benefit is paid only for total disability.

No benefits are paid, because the cause is pre-existing
It is a new disability, so a new elimination period must be satisfied

explanation: A recurrent disability provision treats a relapse from the same cause within a set period (commonly 6 months) as a continuation of the original disability. No new elimination period applies, and the benefit period continues.

prompt: After a crash, pilot Jonah cannot fly, yet the airline will hire him as a dispatcher at his old salary. His individual disability policy defines total disability by his own occupation. Which result follows from that definition?

He is not disabled, because dispatcher work suits his training and replaces his salary
He qualifies only when both flying and dispatch work are impossible
The benefit is reduced dollar for dollar by the salary he earns as a dispatcher

explanation: An own-occupation definition classifies Jonah as totally disabled when he cannot perform the material duties of flying. Taking a dispatcher job at his old salary does not defeat that definition. An any-occupation definition would ask whether dispatch work is reasonably suited to his training.

prompt: Riley's individual disability policy states a 90-day elimination period and a $4,000 monthly benefit, and it pays income only for days of total disability after that period ends. She is totally disabled for exactly 90 days, then returns to full duty. How much income benefit is payable?

options.text: $12,000, three months of the $4,000 benefit with the waiting period ignored
$0, since no disabled day falls after the elimination period
$4,000, treating the whole 90-day wait as one paid benefit month
$8,000, after counting 90 days as three months and dropping only 30

explanation: Payable days equal days disabled minus the elimination period: 90 - 90 = 0. The $4,000 monthly benefit times 0 is $0. The entire disability falls inside the waiting period stated in the policy, so no income benefit accrues.

distractorExplanations.a: Multiplies 3 months by $4,000 to get $12,000 and ignores the wait. All 90 disabled days are used by the 90-day elimination period.
distractorExplanations.c: Treats the 90-day elimination period as one paid month of $4,000. Days inside the stated waiting period are not payable income days.
distractorExplanations.d: Counts 90 days as 3 months, then subtracts only 30 days to leave $8,000. The policy subtracts the full 90-day elimination period, so 90 - 90 = 0.

prompt: A translator returns to freelance work after surgery but earns less than before. Her policy states a residual benefit equal to its $2,000 monthly benefit multiplied by the percent of earnings she lost. She earned $8,000 a month and now earns $2,000. What residual amount is payable?

options.text: $500, from the percent of earnings she still keeps
$2,000, the full benefit, as if she were not working at all
$1,500, three-quarters of the stated monthly benefit
$6,000, the lost wages themselves rather than a share of the $2,000 benefit

explanation: Lost earnings are $8,000 - $2,000 = $6,000. The loss percent is $6,000 / $8,000 = 75 percent, or 3/4. The residual benefit is 3/4 times the $2,000 monthly benefit, which equals $1,500.

distractorExplanations.a: Uses the percent she still earns, $2,000 / $8,000 = 25 percent, times $2,000, which is $500. Residual disability uses the percent lost, not the percent kept.
distractorExplanations.b: Pays the full $2,000 total-disability benefit even though she is working and has lost only part of her pre-disability earnings.
distractorExplanations.d: Pays the $6,000 earnings gap in cash. Residual coverage applies the 75 percent loss to the $2,000 policy benefit, which is $1,500, not the raw wage loss.

prompt: While Marisol stays in her house, a home aide helps her bathe, dress, and eat, and her long-term care policy is paying benefits. Which charge is that policy designed to cover?

options.text: The surgeon's fee for acute hip-replacement surgery performed in a hospital
A monthly check that replaces wages she lost by leaving her job
The premium on a separate disability income policy she still owns
The home aide's charge for help with bathing, dressing, and eating

explanation: Long-term care insurance pays for custodial help with activities of daily living, including bathing, dressing, and eating provided by a home aide. It does not replace wages, pay a surgeon for acute hospital care, or fund the premium on a disability income policy.

distractorExplanations.a: Assigns an acute hospital surgery bill to long-term care. That policy pays for ongoing help with daily living, not the surgeon's fee for fixing a hip.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses long-term care with disability income. A wage-replacement check replaces earnings; it does not pay the aide who helps her bathe and dress.
distractorExplanations.c: Treats another policy's premium as a long-term care expense. The benefit pays the home aide, not the premium on a disability income policy.

prompt: Claims examiner Adele can no longer review files, but she can work full time as a receptionist using her education and experience. Her disability policy uses an any-occupation definition of total disability. When are total disability benefits paid?

options.text: Only when no suited occupation is still possible
As soon as she cannot examine claims, even though receptionist work is suited and available
In full while she works as a receptionist under an own-occupation reading of the policy
Only when a home aide is already helping her bathe, dress, and eat each day

explanation: An any-occupation definition pays total disability benefits only when Adele cannot perform any occupation reasonably suited to her education, training, and experience. Receptionist work meets that test and she can do it, so total disability benefits are not paid.

distractorExplanations.b: Applies an own-occupation test to claims examining. This any-occupation policy does not pay total disability while suited receptionist work remains possible.
distractorExplanations.c: Pays the full benefit during suited work. That result fits an own-occupation definition, which is not the definition this policy uses.
distractorExplanations.d: Imports a long-term care activities trigger. This claim is decided by whether any suited occupation remains, not by bathing or dressing help.

prompt: An applicant compares two disability income policies that are identical except for the elimination period written in each contract. One policy states 30 days and the other states 180 days. Which premium comparison is correct?

options.text: The 30-day contract has the lower premium because its wait is shorter
The 180-day contract is the one with the lower premium
Both contracts carry the same premium because the waiting period is ignored in the rate
The 180-day contract has the higher premium because a longer wait is priced as a penalty

explanation: The 180-day elimination period is 180 - 30 = 150 days longer than the 30-day period. The insured absorbs those extra days before income benefits start, so the insurer expects to pay for fewer days and charges a lower premium for the 180-day policy.

distractorExplanations.a: Reverses the price effect. A 30-day wait is 150 days shorter than 180, so benefits can start sooner and the premium is higher, not lower.
distractorExplanations.c: Ignores the elimination period when setting the price. Changing the stated wait from 30 days to 180 days changes the premium.
distractorExplanations.d: Treats the extra 150 days of waiting as a surcharge. A longer elimination period lowers the premium because benefits start later.

prompt: During recovery a carpenter cannot perform one important duty of his job, but he is not totally disabled. His policy states that it will pay 50 percent of the total disability benefit in that case and will not use an earnings-loss formula. Which benefit is this?

options.text: Residual disability measured by the exact percent of earnings lost
Own-occupation total disability at the full benefit while he still works
Partial disability at a flat half of the total benefit
Presumptive disability, which applies to loss of sight, speech, hearing, or two limbs

explanation: The policy states a flat 50 percent of the total disability benefit. Fifty percent is 50/100 = 1/2, and the policy does not multiply by lost earnings. A flat half benefit while he cannot perform one important duty, but is not totally disabled, is partial disability.

distractorExplanations.a: Describes residual disability, which follows the percent of earnings lost. This policy pays a flat 50 percent and does not use that earnings formula.
distractorExplanations.b: Describes own-occupation total disability at the full benefit. He can still perform some of the job, so the claim is not total disability.
distractorExplanations.d: Describes presumptive disability, which is reserved for specified severe losses such as sight or limbs, not the loss of a single job duty.

prompt: Nora's long-term care contract lists nursing-home room and board, assisted-living care, and adult day care as covered services. Her family places her in adult day care on workdays. Which bill does this contract address?

options.text: Emergency surgery to repair a broken hip in an acute-care hospital
Wage replacement for the income Nora lost when she left her old job
A cash-value loan drawn from a life insurance policy she already owns
The adult day care charge

explanation: Adult day care is named in this long-term care contract, together with nursing-home room and board and assisted living. The contract pays that care bill. Acute surgery, lost wages, and a life-policy loan are not on the covered-services list.

distractorExplanations.a: Names acute hospital surgery. This contract pays nursing-home care, assisted living, and adult day care, not an operation to repair a hip.
distractorExplanations.b: Names lost wages. The services listed in this long-term care contract are care settings, not a check that replaces Nora's income.
distractorExplanations.c: Names a life-insurance cash-value loan. That loan is not nursing-home room and board, assisted living, or adult day care.

prompt: Priya's pharmacist policy pays total disability benefits for 24 months when she cannot do her own job, and pays after that only when she cannot work in any job suited to her training. Which benefit schedule is written in the policy?

options.text: Own-occupation for the first period, then any-occupation
Any-occupation from the first month, skipping the own-occupation period entirely
Residual pay that starts at month 24 and tracks lost pharmacist earnings
A long-term care test based on daily-living help instead of her pharmacy duties

explanation: Own-occupation benefits run for the 24 months stated in the policy, which are months 1 through 24. The any-occupation test begins after that stretch, in month 24 + 1 = 25. The schedule is own-occupation first, then any-occupation.

distractorExplanations.b: Drops the 24-month own-occupation period and starts any-occupation in month 1. The policy uses own-occupation for months 1 through 24, then switches.
distractorExplanations.c: Substitutes a residual earnings benefit at month 24. The policy changes the total-disability test after 24 months; it does not start an earnings-loss formula.
distractorExplanations.d: Substitutes a long-term care activities test. Priya's schedule turns on job duties, first her own pharmacy job and then any job suited to her training.

prompt: Carlos has been totally disabled for 20 days. His disability income policy states a 45-day elimination period and pays no income benefit until that full period has run. How many days of the elimination period remain?

options.text: 20 days, limited to the time he has already been disabled
25 days still left in the elimination period
45 days, because the waiting period starts over from the first day
65 days, adding the 20 days already served to the full 45-day wait

explanation: Days remaining equal the elimination period stated in the policy minus days already disabled: 45 - 20 = 25. No income benefit is paid during those 25 days, because the policy pays nothing until all 45 days have run.

distractorExplanations.a: Stops at the 20 days already served. Those days count toward the wait; they are not the number of days still left, which is 45 - 20.
distractorExplanations.c: Restarts the full 45-day period and erases the 20 days already disabled. Days already served stay credited against the 45.
distractorExplanations.d: Adds 20 + 45 and gets 65. The 20 days reduce the remaining wait; they are not stacked on top of the 45-day period.

prompt: Petra's residual rider states that it pays nothing unless earnings have fallen by at least 20 percent, and that a qualifying loss is then paid as $1,500 times the percent lost. She earned $5,000 a month and now earns $4,500. What is payable?

options.text: $150, which is 10 percent of the $1,500 benefit
$300, which is 20 percent of the $1,500 benefit
Nothing, because the loss misses the stated floor
$1,500, the full monthly benefit for any drop in her monthly earnings

explanation: The earnings drop is $5,000 - $4,500 = $500, and $500 / $5,000 = 10 percent. The rider pays only when the loss is at least 20 percent. Because 10 percent is less than 20 percent, the payment is $0, not 10 percent of $1,500.

distractorExplanations.a: Pays 10 percent of $1,500, which is $150. A 10 percent loss never enters that formula, because the rider requires a loss of at least 20 percent first.
distractorExplanations.b: Pays the 20 percent floor times $1,500, which is $300. The floor is the gate her 10 percent loss missed; it is not the percent her earnings fell.
distractorExplanations.d: Pays the full $1,500 total-disability benefit for a pay cut from $5,000 to $4,500. She is still working, and the residual rider does not treat that cut as total disability.

prompt: Helen receives covered custodial care on each day of a 30-day month. Her long-term care policy states that it pays a $200 indemnity for every day that care is received. What does this policy pay for the month, and for which kind of service?

options.text: $200 for the whole month, because the daily indemnity is paid a single time
$6,000 of lost wages instead of a payment for the custodial care
$0, treating help with bathing and dressing as an expense this policy excludes
$6,000 for the custodial care

explanation: The policy pays a $200 indemnity on each day of covered custodial care. For a 30-day month the amount is 30 x $200 = $6,000. That payment is for the custodial care itself, not for wages Helen lost.

distractorExplanations.a: Pays the $200 daily indemnity only once. Covered care was received on each of 30 days, so the month is 30 x $200 = $6,000, not a single $200 payment.
distractorExplanations.b: Uses the $6,000 figure but calls it lost wages. This long-term care benefit indemnifies custodial care, and it does not replace monthly earnings.
distractorExplanations.c: Denies the claim by treating bathing and dressing help as excluded. Custodial care of that kind is the service this $200 daily indemnity pays for.
